content.text:
You are familiar with triangles and many of their properties from your earlier classes. In Class IX, you have studied congruence of triangles in detail. Recall that two figures are said to be congruent, if they have the same shape and the same size. In this chapter, we shall study about those figures which have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Two figures having the same shape (and not necessarily the same size) are called similar figures. In particular, we shall discuss the similarity of triangles and apply this knowledge in giving a simple proof of Pythagoras Theorem learnt earlier.

Can you guess how heights of mountains (say Mount Everest) or distances of some long distant objects (say moon) have been found out? Do you think these have been measured directly with the help of a measuring tape? In fact, all these heights and distances have been found out using the idea of indirect measurements, which is based on the principle of similarity of figures (you will meet such problems later in this chapter and in later chapters).

media.title: Similar vs Congruent: Passport Photo and Map Analogy
media.description: A 2D animated video showing a 3 cm x 4 cm passport photo enlarging frame-by-frame to a 9 cm x 12 cm poster. Annotations '9 = 3 x 3' and '12 = 4 x 3' appear alongside each side as the enlargement animates. On-screen text reads 'Same shape, scale factor 3 - similar.' A second scene shows two photos of the same person: one at age 10 and one at age 40, both the same size but visibly different shapes. Text reads 'Same size, different shape - not similar.' A final scene shows the formal definition: 'Similar figures: same shape, not necessarily the same size.' Circles of different radii, squares of different sides, and equilateral triangles of different sizes appear as three rows with the label 'similar' beneath each row.
media.teaching_notes:
WHEN: Play this video BEFORE the student attempts the Exercise 6.1 fill-in-the-blank questions and AFTER the student has looked at the textbook figures of circles, squares, and equilateral triangles. The video consolidates the distinction between congruence and similarity.
WHAT TO PAUSE AT: (1) Pause at the end of Scene 2 (approx. 90s) before Scene 3 begins. Ask: 'The two photos are the same size - why are they not similar?' Prompt students to articulate the shape-change reason. (2) Pause at the Final scene (approx. 145s) before the answer is revealed. Ask: 'Are all isosceles triangles similar to each other? What would you need to check?'
WHAT TO ASK: At the Scene 3 pause, ask 'What would you do next to decide if two figures are similar?' - this is the attempt-before-reveal moment for the definition check. After the video, ask: 'Give one example of two figures that are similar but not congruent from your daily life.'

topics.summary: Same shape, not necessarily the same size

content.text:
In Class IX, you have seen that all circles with the same radii are congruent, all squares with the same side lengths are congruent and all equilateral triangles with the same side lengths are congruent.

Now consider any two (or more) circles (see the figure). Are they congruent? Since all of them do not have the same radius, they are not congruent to each other. Note that some are congruent and some are not, but all of them have the same shape. So they all are, what we call, similar. Two similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Therefore, all circles are similar. What about two (or more) squares or two (or more) equilateral triangles (see the figure)? As observed in the case of circles, here also all squares are similar and all equilateral triangles are similar.

From the above, we can say that all congruent figures are similar but the similar figures need not be congruent.

Can a circle and a square be similar? Can a triangle and a square be similar? These questions can be answered by just looking at the figures. Evidently these figures are not similar. (Why?)

media.title: Two Conditions for Polygon Similarity: Animated Walkthrough
media.description: A 2D animated video opening with a photographer enlarging a 35 mm negative to a 55 mm print. Each side of the print is annotated with the ratio 55/35; angle arcs on the print show that corresponding angles are preserved. On-screen text displays both similarity conditions. A second scene shows a square and a rectangle side by side: right-angle marks at all corners, sides 3 and 3 on the square and 3 and 4 on the rectangle. Red annotations show the unequal ratios 3/3 = 1 and 3/4 ≠ 1, and the verdict 'Not similar' appears. A third scene shows a square and a rhombus with equal side marks but different angle arcs; equal side marks are shown in green, unequal angles in red, and the verdict 'Not similar' appears. A final screen states the transitivity remark as on-screen text.
media.teaching_notes:
WHEN: Play this video AFTER students have seen the textbook counter-example figures (Figs. 6.6 and 6.7) and BEFORE they attempt the polygon-similarity-condition checker interactive tool. It reinforces the two-condition rule through the positive photographer example and two negative examples.
WHAT TO PAUSE AT: (1) Pause at approximately 100s (end of Scene 2, after the square-rectangle counter-example) and ask: 'Can you describe a situation where corresponding sides are proportional but the figures are still not similar?' This is the attempt-before-reveal moment for the square-rhombus scene. (2) Pause at the end of Scene 3 (approx. 155s) and ask: 'What single statement describes when exactly two polygons are similar?'
WHAT TO ASK: At the Scene 2 pause, ask 'What would you do next to test a new pair of polygons - which condition would you check first?' After the video, ask students to write both conditions in their own words without looking at the screen.
media.generation_prompt:
[Duration]: 180 seconds.
[Style]: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal.
[Scene sequence]: 4 scenes.
  Scene 1 (0-50s): Problem statement - a 35 mm film frame enlarges to a 55 mm print. Each side ratio '55/35' appears in Orange alongside the sides. Angle arcs on both frames are shown with matching coloured symbols. On-screen text in Navy Blue states the two similarity conditions: '(i) Corresponding angles equal AND (ii) Corresponding sides proportional.' Narrator: 'Notice how both conditions hold simultaneously - angles are preserved and every side grew by the same ratio.'
  Scene 2 (50-100s): Setup - a square (3 x 3) and a rectangle (3 x 4) appear side by side. Right-angle marks at all corners in Navy Blue. Side ratios computed: 3/3 = 1 in green, 3/4 = 0.75 in red. On-screen annotation: 'Condition (i) holds, condition (ii) fails. NOT similar.' Narrator: 'The key insight here is that equal angles alone are not enough. The side ratios must also match.' Pause prompt: 'Before the next example - can you think of two figures where the side ratios match but the angles differ?'
  Scene 3 (100-155s): Each step - a square (side 3 cm) and a rhombus (side 3 cm, acute angle 60°) appear. Equal side marks on all eight sides in Navy Blue. Angle arcs: square has four 90° arcs in green; rhombus has two 60° and two 120° arcs in red. On-screen: 'Condition (ii) holds, condition (i) fails. NOT similar.' Narrator: 'Equal side lengths - yet different shape. Angles must also match.'
  Final scene (155-180s): Check - transitivity remark appears as on-screen text: 'If P1 ∼ P2 and P2 ∼ P3, then P1 ∼ P3.' Narrator summarises: 'Both conditions must hold together for polygon similarity.'
[Narration style]: Calm, instructional.
[Music]: None.
[Visual elements]: Color-coded conditions (green for passing condition, red for failing), matching arc symbols, clean equations in Navy Blue and Orange, white background.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch with pencil and paper. Before Scene 3 begins, predict an example where side ratios are equal but angles are not, and write it down.

content.text:
What can you say about the two quadrilaterals ABCD and PQRS in the figure? Are they similar? These figures appear to be similar but we cannot be certain about it. Therefore, we must have some definition of similarity of figures and based on this definition some rules to decide whether the two given figures are similar or not. For this, let us look at some photographs.

You will at once say that they are the photographs of the same monument (Taj Mahal) but are in different sizes. Would you say that the three photographs are similar? Yes, they are.

What can you say about the two photographs of the same size of the same person one at the age of 10 years and the other at the age of 40 years? Are these photographs similar? These photographs are of the same size but certainly they are not of the same shape. So, they are not similar.

What does the photographer do when she prints photographs of different sizes from the same negative? You must have heard about the stamp size, passport size and postcard size photographs. She generally takes a photograph on a small size film, say of 35mm size and then enlarges it into a bigger size, say 45mm (or 55mm). Thus, if we consider any line segment in the smaller photograph (figure), its corresponding line segment in the bigger photograph (figure) will be 45/35 or 55/35 of that of the line segment. This really means that every line segment of the smaller photograph is enlarged (increased) in the ratio 35:45 (or 35:55). It can also be said that every line segment of the bigger photograph is reduced (decreased) in the ratio 45:35 (or 55:35). Further, if you consider inclinations (or angles) between any pair of corresponding line segments in the two photographs of different sizes, you shall see that these inclinations (or angles) are always equal. This is the essence of the similarity of two figures and in particular of two polygons. We say that:

This really means that every line segment of the smaller photograph is enlarged (increased) in the ratio 35:45 (or 35:55). It can also be said that every line segment of the bigger photograph is reduced (decreased) in the ratio 45:35 (or 55:35). Further, if you consider inclinations (or angles) between any pair of corresponding line segments in the two photographs of different sizes, you shall see that these inclinations (or angles) are always equal. This is the essence of the similarity of two figures and in particular of two polygons. We say that:

content.text:
In order to understand similarity of figures more clearly, let us perform the following activity:

Activity : Place a lighted bulb at a point O on the ceiling and directly below it a table in your classroom. Let us cut a polygon, say a quadrilateral ABCD, from a plane cardboard and place this cardboard parallel to the ground between the lighted bulb and the table. Then a shadow of ABCD is cast on the table. Mark the outline of this shadow as A'B'C'D' (see the figure).

Note that the quadrilateral A'B'C'D' is an enlargement (or magnification) of the quadrilateral ABCD. This is because of the property of light that light propagates in a straight line. You may also note that A' lies on ray OA, B' lies on ray OB, C' lies on OC and D' lies on OD. Thus, quadrilaterals ABCD and A'B'C'D' are of the same shape but of different sizes.

So, quadrilateral ABCD is similar to quadrilateral A'B'C'D'. We can also say that quadrilateral A'B'C'D' is similar to the quadrilateral ABCD.

Here, you can also note that vertex A corresponds to vertex A', vertex B corresponds to vertex B', vertex C corresponds to vertex C' and vertex D corresponds to vertex D'. Symbolically, these correspondences are represented as A↔A', B↔B', C↔C' and D↔D'. By actually measuring the angles and the sides of the two quadrilaterals, you may verify that
(i) ∠A = ∠A', ∠B = ∠B', ∠C = ∠C', ∠D = ∠D' and
(ii) AB/A'B' = BC/B'C' = CD/C'D' = DA/D'A'.

This again emphasises that two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) all the corresponding angles are equal and (ii) all the corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).

From the above, you can easily say that the quadrilaterals ABCD and PQRS in the figure are similar.

You may note that in the two quadrilaterals (a square and a rectangle) in the figure, corresponding angles are equal, but their corresponding sides are not in the same ratio. So, the two quadrilaterals are not similar. Thus, either of the above two conditions (i) and (ii) of similarity of two polygons is not sufficient for them to be similar.

content.text:
Q. Why can a circle and a square never be similar, or a triangle and a square?
A. Similar figures must have the same shape. A circle has no corners and no straight sides, while a square has four corners and four straight sides, so no enlargement or reduction can turn one into the other. A triangle and a square have different numbers of sides, so their sides and angles cannot even be paired off.

content.text:
Q. Two squares of sides 2 cm and 2 cm are congruent. Are they also similar?
A. Yes. Their corresponding angles are all 90° and their corresponding sides are in the ratio 1 : 1. Every pair of congruent figures is similar, with scale factor 1.

media.title: Thales of Miletus and the Discovery of BPT
media.description: A 2D animated video opening with a silhouette figure of Thales beside a stylised Mediterranean coastline. On-screen text reads 'Thales (c. 624-546 BCE)' and the statement 'The ratio of any two corresponding sides in equiangular triangles is always the same.' The second segment shows the Activity 2 construction animating step by step: angle XAY drawn, then five equally spaced points P, Q, D, R, B marked on ray AX with equal-spacing tick marks, then line BC drawn through B intersecting AY at C, then line DE through D parallel to BC intersecting AY at E. Ratio annotations AD/DB = 3/2 and AE/EC = 3/2 appear alongside the figure. The construction then repeats with a different ratio (AD/DB = 4/1) and AE/EC is shown to equal 4/1 again.
media.teaching_notes:
WHEN: Play this video BEFORE the student uses the interactive BPT discovery slider tool, to set the historical context and demonstrate the Activity 2 construction process.
WHAT TO PAUSE AT: (1) Pause at approximately 110s (after the first ratio AD/DB = AE/EC = 3/2 is shown) and ask: 'What ratio would you predict for AE/EC if AD/DB were changed to 4/1? Write your prediction before the video confirms it.' This is the attempt-before-reveal moment. (2) Pause at the end of Scene 2 (approx. 120s) before the repeated construction and ask: 'Does the position of D on AB matter? Would the result change if D were closer to A?'
WHAT TO ASK: After the video, ask: 'What is the name of the theorem illustrated, and what are the two parts of the result it states?' Encourage students to write the BPT in their own words.

content.text:
What can you say about the similarity of two triangles?

You may recall that triangle is also a polygon. So, we can state the same conditions for the similarity of two triangles. That is:
Two triangles are similar, if
(i) their corresponding angles are equal and
(ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).

Note that if corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, then they are known as equiangular triangles. A famous Greek mathematician Thales gave an important truth relating to two equiangular triangles which is as follows:
The ratio of any two corresponding sides in two equiangular triangles is always the same.
It is believed that he had used a result called the Basic Proportionality Theorem (now known as the Thales Theorem) for the same.

To understand the Basic Proportionality Theorem, let us perform the following activity:

Activity : Draw any angle XAY and on its one arm AX, mark points (say five points) P, Q, D, R and B such that AP = PQ = QD = DR = RB.
Now, through B, draw any line intersecting arm AY at C (see the figure).
Also, through the point D, draw a line parallel to BC to intersect AC at E. Do you observe from your constructions that AD/DB = 3/2? Measure AE and EC. What about AE/EC? Observe that AE/EC is also equal to 3/2. Thus, you can see that in △ABC, DE ∥ BC and AD/DB = AE/EC. Is it a coincidence? No, it is due to the following theorem (known as the Basic Proportionality Theorem):

content.text:
We are given a triangle ABC in which a line parallel to side BC intersects other two sides AB and AC at D and E respectively (see the figure).
We need to prove that AD/DB = AE/EC.
Let us join BE and CD and then draw DM ⊥ AC and EN ⊥ AB.
Now, area of △ADE (= 1/2 × base × height) = 1/2 × AD × EN.
Recall from Class IX, that area of △ADE is denoted as ar(ADE).
So, ar(ADE) = 1/2 × AD × EN
Similarly, ar(BDE) = 1/2 × DB × EN,
ar(ADE) = 1/2 × AE × DM and ar(DEC) = 1/2 × EC × DM.
Therefore, ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = (AD × EN)/(DB × EN) = AD/DB ... (1)
and ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = (AE × DM)/(EC × DM) = AE/EC ... (2)
Note that △BDE and DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels BC and DE.
So, ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) ... (3)
Therefore, from (1), (2) and (3), we have :
AD/DB = AE/EC

content.text:
Is the converse of this theorem also true? To examine this, let us perform the following activity:

Activity : Draw an angle XAY on your notebook and on ray AX, mark points B₁, B₂, B₃, B₄ and B such that AB₁ = B₁B₂ = B₂B₃ = B₃B₄ = B₄B.
Similarly, on ray AY, mark points C₁, C₂, C₃, C₄ and C such that AC₁ = C₁C₂ = C₂C₃ = C₃C₄ = C₄C. Then join B₁C₁ and BC (see the figure).
Note that AB₁/B₁B = AC₁/C₁C = 1/4. You can also see that lines B₁C₁ and BC are parallel to each other, i.e., B₁C₁ ∥ BC ... (1)

This theorem can be proved by taking a line DE such that AD/DB = AE/EC and assuming that DE is not parallel to BC (see the figure).
If DE is not parallel to BC, draw a line DE' parallel to BC.

content.text:
Q. Why is AD/DB = AE'/E'C?
A. DE' is parallel to BC and meets the sides AB and AC of △ABC at D and E', so the basic proportionality theorem gives AD/DB = AE'/E'C.

Q. Why is AD/DB = AE'/E'C?
A. DE' is parallel to BC and meets the sides AB and AC of △ABC at D and E', so the basic proportionality theorem gives AD/DB = AE'/E'C.

content.text:
Q. Why is AE/EC = AE'/E'C?
A. We are given AD/DB = AE/EC, and we have just found AD/DB = AE'/E'C. Both ratios equal AD/DB, so they equal each other.
content.publication_text:
Q. Why is AE/EC = AE'/E'C?
A. We are given AD/DB = AE/EC, and we have just found AD/DB = AE'/E'C. Both ratios equal AD/DB, so they equal each other.

content.text:
Q. Why must E and E' coincide?
A. Adding 1 to both sides gives (AE + EC)/EC = (AE' + E'C)/E'C, that is, AC/EC = AC/E'C. So EC = E'C. Both points lie on AC at the same distance from C, so they are the same point, and DE is the line DE', which is parallel to BC.

content.text:
It is given that PS/SQ = PT/TR
So, ST ∥ QR (Converse of the basic proportionality theorem)
Therefore, ∠PST = ∠PQR (Corresponding angles) ... (1)
Also, it is given that
∠PST = ∠PRQ ... (2)
So, ∠PRQ = ∠PQR [From (1) and (2)]
Therefore, PQ = PR (Sides opposite the equal angles)
i.e., PQR is an isosceles triangle.

media.title: Similarity Notation Diagram: Triangle ABC similar to Triangle DEF with Vertex Correspondence
media.description: Two triangles drawn side by side. Left triangle ABC has vertex A at top, B at bottom-left, C at bottom-right. Right triangle DEF has the same orientation but is larger. Curved correspondence arrows connect A to D, B to E, and C to F. The symbolic statement 'Triangle ABC ~ Triangle DEF' is printed prominently above. Equal angle pairs at A and D, B and E, C and F are marked with matching arcs. The side-ratio equation AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD is written below. An incorrectly ordered statement 'Triangle ABC ~ Triangle EDF' is shown crossed out with the note 'incorrect vertex order'.
media.teaching_notes: Display this diagram immediately after introducing the symbol ~. Point to the matching arcs to show how the vertex correspondence determines which angles are equal, and to the crossed-out statement to highlight the most common notation error. Ask the student to read the correspondence aloud: 'A goes to D, B goes to E, C goes to F'.

media.title: Proof Sketch Animation: AAA Criterion
media.description: A 2D animated video showing the proof sketch of Theorem 6.3. The opening scene shows triangles ABC and DEF with equal angle arcs at corresponding vertices: angle A = angle D (Navy Blue), angle B = angle E (Orange), angle C = angle F (Light Blue). Step 2 animates the auxiliary cut: a point P is marked on DE at distance DP = AB, and point Q is marked on DF at DQ = AC; line PQ is drawn. Step 3 highlights triangle ABC and triangle DPQ with matching colours and writes 'congruent by SAS' with the two equal sides and equal included angle identified. Step 4 shows angle B = angle P derived from congruency, then PQ parallel to EF established. Step 5 applies Theorem 6.1 to give AB/DE = AC/DF. Step 6 states the AA corollary.
media.teaching_notes:
WHEN: Play this video AFTER the student has explored the AAA activity using the interactive angle slider and BEFORE the student reads the formal proof. The animation makes the cut DP = AB construction step visually logical before the algebra.
WHAT TO PAUSE AT: (1) Pause at approximately 60s (after P and Q are cut but before the congruency is established) and ask: 'We have cut DP = AB and DQ = AC. What angle is shared between triangle ABC and triangle DPQ? Can you name the congruency criterion?' This is the attempt-before-reveal moment. (2) Pause at approximately 95s (after congruency is shown) and ask: 'We now know angle B = angle P. And we know angle B = angle E from the given. What does this tell us about the relationship between PQ and EF?'
WHAT TO ASK: After the video, ask: 'Why does this proof work only for triangles and not for quadrilaterals with equal angles?'

[Duration]: 200 seconds.
[Style]: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal.
[Scene sequence]: 6 scenes.
  Scene 1 (0-25s): Problem statement - triangle ABC and triangle DEF appear side by side. Equal angle arcs: ∠A = ∠D (Navy Blue), ∠B = ∠E (Orange), ∠C = ∠F (Light Blue). Text: 'Given: all three pairs of angles equal. Prove: sides proportional.' Narrator: 'Three equal angle pairs - can we prove the sides must also be proportional?'
  Scene 2 (25-60s): Setup - within triangle DEF, point P animates onto DE with DP = AB (equal-segment marks in Orange). Point Q animates onto DF with DQ = AC (equal-segment marks in Navy Blue). PQ drawn in grey dashes. Text: 'Cut DP = AB, DQ = AC. Join PQ.'
  Scene 3 (60-95s): Each step - triangle ABC (light pale yellow) and triangle DPQ (Light Blue) highlighted. SAS conditions: DP = AB (construction), ∠D = ∠A (given), DQ = AC (construction). 'Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle DPQ by SAS' written. Therefore ∠B = ∠P derived. Narrator: 'What would you do next to show PQ is parallel to EF?' Pause prompt.
  Scene 4 (95-135s): Each step - ∠P = ∠E (since ∠B = ∠P and ∠B = ∠E from given). Therefore PQ ∥ EF by converse of corresponding angles. Theorem 6.1 applied in triangle DEF: DP/PE = DQ/QF → AB/DE = AC/DF. Similarly AB/DE = BC/EF.
  Scene 5 (135-175s): Each step - all three ratios: AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD concluded. Triangle ABC ~ Triangle DEF stated. Narrator: 'The key insight here is that the auxiliary congruent triangle DPQ inside DEF created the parallel line needed to apply BPT.'
  Final scene (175-200s): Check - AA corollary stated: 'Two equal angle pairs are sufficient (angle sum gives the third).' Narrator: 'What is the minimum number of angle equalities needed to conclude similarity?'
[Narration style]: Calm, instructional.
[Music]: None.
[Visual elements]: Equal angle arcs in three colours, auxiliary cut animation in Orange and Navy Blue, shaded congruent triangles, BPT arrows in Light Blue, white background.

media.description: A 2D animated proof video for Theorem 6.4. The opening scene shows Activity 5 triangles: triangle ABC with AB = 3, BC = 6, CA = 8 and triangle DEF with DE = 4.5, EF = 9, FD = 12. Side ratios AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD = 2/3 are computed and displayed. Step 2 animates the cut DP = AB and DQ = AC inside triangle DEF with equal-segment marks. Step 3 derives the ratio DP/PE = DQ/QF from the proportional sides, then invokes Theorem 6.2 to show PQ parallel to EF. WHEN: Play this video AFTER the student has completed Activity 5 measurements and BEFORE the interactive SSS proof step explorer. The animation makes the DP/PE = DQ/QF algebraic step explicit, which is the most commonly skipped step.
WHAT TO PAUSE AT: (1) Pause at approximately 70s (after DP and DQ are cut but before Theorem 6.2 is invoked) and ask: 'We know DP/PE = DQ/QF. Which theorem can we use to conclude something about line PQ?' This is the attempt-before-reveal moment. (2) Pause at approximately 115s (after PQ ∥ EF is established) and ask: 'PQ is parallel to EF. What does this tell us about angles P and E?'
WHAT TO ASK: After the video, ask: 'At which step did we first use the fact that all three side ratios are equal rather than just two of them? Could the proof work with only two proportional sides?'

content.text:
Earlier, we stated that two triangles are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion). That is, in △ABC and △DEF, if
(i) ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F and
(ii) AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD, then the two triangles are similar (see the figure).

Here, you can see that A corresponds to D, B corresponds to E and C corresponds to F. Symbolically, we write the similarity of these two triangles as '△ABC ~ △DEF' and read it as 'triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF'. The symbol '~' stands for 'is similar to'. Recall that you have used the symbol '≅' for 'is congruent to' in Class IX.

It must be noted that as done in the case of congruency of two triangles, the similarity of two triangles should also be expressed symbolically, using correct correspondence of their vertices. For example, for the triangles ABC and DEF in the figure, we cannot write △ABC ~ △EDF or △ABC ~ △FED. However, we can write △BAC ~ △EDF.

Now a natural question arises : For checking the similarity of two triangles, say ABC and DEF, should we always look for all the equality relations of their corresponding angles (∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F) and all the equality relations of the ratios of their corresponding sides (AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD)? Let us examine. You may recall that in Class IX, you have obtained some criteria for congruency of two triangles involving only three pairs of corresponding parts (or elements) of the two triangles. Here also, let us make an attempt to arrive at certain criteria for similarity of two triangles involving relationship between less number of pairs of corresponding parts of the two triangles, instead of all the six pairs of corresponding parts.

concepts.concept_name: Writing a similarity the right way round

content.text:
For this, let us perform the following activity:

Activity : Draw two line segments BC and EF of two different lengths, say 3 cm and 5 cm respectively. Then, at the points B and C respectively, construct angles PBC and QCB of some measures, say, 60° and 40°. Also, at the points E and F, construct angles REF and SFE of 60° and 40° respectively (see the figure).

Let rays BP and CQ intersect each other at A and rays ER and FS intersect each other at D. In the two triangles ABC and DEF, you can see that ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F and ∠A = ∠D. That is, corresponding angles of these two triangles are equal. Note that BC/EF = 3/5 = 0.6. On measuring AB, DE, CA and FD, you will find that AB/DE and CA/FD are also equal to 0.6 (or nearly equal to 0.6, if there is some error in the measurement). Thus, AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD. You can repeat this activity by constructing several pairs of triangles having their corresponding angles equal. Every time, you will find that their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion). This activity leads us to the following criterion for similarity of two triangles.

content.text:
If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion) and hence the two triangles are similar.
This criterion is referred to as the AAA (Angle-Angle-Angle) criterion of similarity of two triangles.

i.e., AB/DE = AC/DF (Why?)
Similarly, AB/DE = BC/EF and so AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF.

content.text:
If two angles of a triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then by the angle sum property of a triangle their third angles will also be equal. Therefore, AAA similarity criterion can also be stated as follows:
If two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are similar.
This may be referred to as the AA similarity criterion for two triangles.

concepts.concept_name: Why equal angles force equal ratios

content.text:
You have seen above that if the three angles of one triangle are respectively equal to the three angles of another triangle, then their corresponding sides are proportional (i.e., in the same ratio). What about the converse of this statement? Is the converse true? In other words, if the sides of a triangle are respectively proportional to the sides of another triangle, is it true that their corresponding angles are equal? Let us examine it through an activity :

Activity : Draw two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB = 3 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 8 cm, DE = 4.5 cm, EF = 9 cm and FD = 12 cm (see the figure).
So, you have : AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD = 2/3.
Now measure ∠A, ∠B, ∠C, ∠D, ∠E and ∠F. You will observe that ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F, i.e., the corresponding angles of the two triangles are equal.

Let us now recall the various criteria for congruency of two triangles learnt in Class IX. You may observe that SSS similarity criterion can be compared with the SSS congruency criterion. This suggests us to look for a similarity criterion comparable to SAS congruency criterion of triangles. For this, let us perform an activity.

Activity : Draw two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB = 2 cm, ∠A = 50°, AC = 4 cm, DE = 3 cm, ∠D = 50° and DF = 6 cm (see the figure).
Here, you may observe that AB/DE = AC/DF = 2/3 and ∠A (included between the sides AB and AC) = ∠D (included between the sides DE and DF). That is, one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and sides including these angles are in the same ratio (i.e., proportion). Now let us measure ∠B, ∠C, ∠E and ∠F.

content.text:
Q. In the AAA sketch, why is △ABC ≅ △DPQ, and how do we get ∠B = ∠P = ∠E and PQ ∥ EF?
A. DP = AB, DQ = AC and ∠D = ∠A, so the triangles are congruent by SAS. Then ∠B = ∠P as corresponding parts. We are given ∠B = ∠E, so ∠P = ∠E. These are corresponding angles for the lines PQ and EF cut by DE, so PQ ∥ EF.
content.publication_text:
Q. In the AAA sketch, why is △ABC ≅ △DPQ, and how do we get ∠B = ∠P = ∠E and PQ ∥ EF?
A. DP = AB, DQ = AC and ∠D = ∠A, so the triangles are congruent by SAS. Then ∠B = ∠P as corresponding parts. We are given ∠B = ∠E, so ∠P = ∠E. These are corresponding angles for the lines PQ and EF cut by DE, so PQ ∥ EF.

content.text:
Q. In the AAA sketch, why is DP/PE = DQ/QF, and why does that give AB/DE = AC/DF?
A. PQ ∥ EF in △DEF, so the basic proportionality theorem gives DP/PE = DQ/QF. Turning both ratios over and adding 1 gives DE/DP = DF/DQ, so DP/DE = DQ/DF. Since DP = AB and DQ = AC, this is AB/DE = AC/DF.
content.publication_text:
Q. In the AAA sketch, why is DP/PE = DQ/QF, and why does that give AB/DE = AC/DF?
A. PQ ∥ EF in △DEF, so the basic proportionality theorem gives DP/PE = DQ/QF. Turning both ratios over and adding 1 gives DE/DP = DF/DQ, so DP/DE = DQ/DF. Since DP = AB and DQ = AC, this is AB/DE = AC/DF.

content.text:
Q. In the SSS sketch, how do we see DP/PE = DQ/QF and PQ ∥ EF?
A. We are given AB/DE = CA/FD, that is DP/DE = DQ/DF. Then DP/(DE − DP) = DQ/(DF − DQ), which is DP/PE = DQ/QF. By the converse of the basic proportionality theorem, PQ ∥ EF.
content.publication_text:
Q. In the SSS sketch, how do we see DP/PE = DQ/QF and PQ ∥ EF?
A. We are given AB/DE = CA/FD, that is DP/DE = DQ/DF. Then DP/(DE − DP) = DQ/(DF − DQ), which is DP/PE = DQ/QF. By the converse of the basic proportionality theorem, PQ ∥ EF.

content.text:
Q. In the SSS sketch, why is DP/DE = DQ/DF = BC/EF, why is BC = PQ, and why is △ABC ≅ △DPQ?
A. DP/DE = AB/DE, and AB/DE = BC/EF is given. From DP/DE = DQ/DF = PQ/EF we then get PQ/EF = BC/EF, so BC = PQ. Now AB = DP, AC = DQ and BC = PQ, so the triangles are congruent by SSS.
content.publication_text:
Q. In the SSS sketch, why is DP/DE = DQ/DF = BC/EF, why is BC = PQ, and why is △ABC ≅ △DPQ?
A. DP/DE = AB/DE, and AB/DE = BC/EF is given. From DP/DE = DQ/DF = PQ/EF we then get PQ/EF = BC/EF, so BC = PQ. Now AB = DP, AC = DQ and BC = PQ, so the triangles are congruent by SSS.

content.text:
Q. In the SSS sketch, how do we finish with ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F?
A. From the congruence, ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠P and ∠C = ∠Q. From the parallel lines, ∠P = ∠E and ∠Q = ∠F. So ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F.
content.publication_text:
Q. In the SSS sketch, how do we finish with ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F?
A. From the congruence, ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠P and ∠C = ∠Q. From the parallel lines, ∠P = ∠E and ∠Q = ∠F. So ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F.

content.text:

A. AB/DE = AC/DF means DP/DE = DQ/DF, so DP/PE = DQ/QF and, by the converse of the basic proportionality theorem, PQ ∥ EF. DP = AB, DQ = AC and ∠D = ∠A give the congruence by SAS. Then ∠B = ∠P = ∠E and ∠C = ∠Q = ∠F (corresponding angles, as PQ ∥ EF), and ∠A = ∠D, so the triangles are similar by the AAA criterion.

content.text: A girl of height 90 cm is walking away from the base of a lamp-post at a speed of 1.2 m/s. If the lamp is 3.6 m above the ground, find the length of her shadow after 4 seconds.

content.publication_text: A girl of height 90 cm is walking away from the base of a lamp-post at a speed of 1.2 m/s. If the lamp is 3.6 m above the ground, find the length of her shadow after 4 seconds.

content.text:
Let AB denote the lamp-post and CD the girl after walking for 4 seconds away from the lamp-post (see the figure). From the figure, you can see that DE is the shadow of the girl. Let DE be x metres.
Now, BD = 1.2 m × 4 = 4.8 m.
Note that in △ABE and △CDE,
∠B = ∠D (Each is of 90° because lamp-post as well as the girl are standing vertical to the ground)
and ∠E = ∠E (Same angle)
So, △ABE ~ △CDE (AA similarity criterion)
Therefore, BE/DE = AB/CD
(4.8 + x)/x = 3.6/0.9 (90 cm = 90/100 m = 0.9 m)
i.e., 4.8 + x = 4x
i.e., 3x = 4.8
i.e., x = 1.6
So, the shadow of the girl after walking for 4 seconds is 1.6 m long.

(ii) CM/RN = AB/PQ
(iii) △CMB ~ △RNQ

content.text:
(i) △ABC ~ △PQR (Given)
So, AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP ... (1)
and ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q and ∠C = ∠R ... (2)
But AB = 2 AM and PQ = 2 PN
(As CM and RN are medians)
So, from (1), 2AM/2PN = CA/RP
i.e., AM/PN = CA/RP ... (3)
Also, ∠MAC = ∠NPR [From (2)] ... (4)
So, from (3) and (4),
△AMC ~ △PNR (SAS similarity) ... (5)
(ii) From (5), CM/RN = CA/RP ... (6)
But CA/RP = AB/PQ [From (1)] ... (7)
Therefore, CM/RN = AB/PQ [From (6) and (7)] ... (8)
(iii) Again, AB/PQ = BC/QR [From (1)]
Therefore, CM/RN = BC/QR [From (8)] ... (9)
Also, CM/RN = AB/PQ = 2BM/2QN
i.e., CM/RN = BM/QN ... (10)
Therefore, CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN [From (9) and (10)]
Therefore, △CMB ~ △RNQ (SSS similarity)

learning_objectives.objective_text: Apply AAA, SSS, and SAS similarity criteria to identify similar triangle pairs and find unknown angles or side ratios in geometric figures.
Solve real-world indirect measurement problems involving heights and shadows using the AA similarity criterion for triangles.
Translate a real-world geometric scenario into a similar triangle relationship and calculate unknown lengths through proportionality.

Apply SAS similarity to prove △AMC ∼ △PNR using the median-derived proportionality AM/PN = CA/RP and the included angle equality ∠MAC = ∠NPR, then chain the result to prove CM/RN = AB/PQ and to apply SSS similarity to prove △CMB ∼ △RNQ.

media.title: Recap: All Five Similarity Criteria in 120 Seconds
media.description: A 2D animated recap video showing nine summary points sequentially, each displayed for approximately 10 to 12 seconds. Each point is accompanied by a small diagram: two triangles of different sizes for the similar figures definition, a BPT triangle with DE parallel to BC, a contradiction diagram for the Converse BPT, two equiangular triangles with matching arcs for AAA, two triangles with two matching arcs for AA, two triangles with three ratio marks for SSS, two triangles with one ratio pair and one included angle for SAS, and two right triangles with hypotenuse marks for RHS. The final 15 seconds show a comparison row placing each similarity criterion beside its congruency counterpart from Class IX, with the key difference 'proportional sides vs equal sides' highlighted in Orange.
media.teaching_notes:
WHEN: Play this video at the END of Chapter 6 as a final review, ideally AFTER students have completed Exercise 6.3 and BEFORE any end-of-chapter test. It serves as a rapid retrieval practice run through all nine key results.
WHAT TO PAUSE AT: (1) Pause at approximately 45s (after Polygon Similarity, Point 3, before BPT) and ask: 'Without looking, can you state the two conditions for polygon similarity?' This is the attempt-before-reveal moment for the BPT definition. (2) Pause at approximately 135s (at the comparison table) and ask: 'For each similarity criterion (AAA, SSS, SAS), what is the corresponding congruency criterion from Class IX? Write them all before the final scene shows the comparison.'
WHAT TO ASK: After the video, ask: 'Which criterion is unique to triangles and does not extend to general polygons? Why does it work only for triangles?' This targets the AAA criterion and the polygon counter-examples from Segment 1.

[Duration]: 180 seconds.
[Style]: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, sequential reveal at a steady pace.
[Scene sequence]: 10 scenes (9 summary points + 1 comparison).
  Scene 1 (0-15s): Point 1 - two triangles of different sizes. Text: 'Similar figures: same shape, not necessarily same size.' Small label 'scale factor k'. Narrator: 'Two figures are similar if they have the same shape.'
  Scene 2 (15-30s): Point 2 - congruent pair highlighted with ≅ symbol inside similar pair. Text: 'All congruent figures are similar. Converse is NOT true.' Narrator: 'Congruence implies similarity, but not the reverse.'
  Scene 3 (30-45s): Point 3 - polygon similarity: two quadrilaterals with angle arcs and side-ratio marks. Text: 'Polygon similarity: (i) equal angles AND (ii) proportional sides.'
  Scene 4 (45-60s): Point 4 - BPT triangle: DE ∥ BC, ratios AD/DB = AE/EC. Text: 'Theorem 6.1 (BPT): parallel line divides two sides proportionally.'
  Scene 5 (60-75s): Point 5 - Converse BPT: DE with equal ratios implying parallel. Text: 'Theorem 6.2 (Converse BPT): equal ratios imply parallel line.'
  Scene 6 (75-90s): Point 6 - AAA: two triangles with three matching angle arcs. Text: 'Theorem 6.3 (AAA): three equal angle pairs → similar.'
  Scene 7 (90-105s): Point 7 - AA corollary: two matching arcs only. Text: 'AA corollary: two equal angle pairs sufficient (angle sum gives third).'
  Scene 8 (105-120s): Point 8 - SSS: three pairs of side-ratio tick marks. Text: 'Theorem 6.4 (SSS): three proportional side pairs → similar.'
  Scene 9 (120-135s): Point 9 - SAS: one included angle arc and two ratio marks. Text: 'Theorem 6.5 (SAS): one equal included angle + two proportional sides → similar.' RHS noted briefly.
  Final scene (135-180s): Check - comparison table: similarity criteria on left vs congruency criteria on right. Key difference highlighted in Orange: 'Similarity: proportional sides. Congruency: equal sides.' Narrator: 'The key insight here is that similarity is congruency with a scale factor k. When k = 1, similarity becomes congruency.'
[Narration style]: Calm, brisk recap pace.
[Music]: None.
[Visual elements]: Consistent clean diagrams, Navy Blue for theorems, Orange for key differences, Light Blue for angle arcs, grey tick marks, white background.

topics.summary: Chapter summary; A note on right triangles

content.text:
In this chapter you have studied the following points :
1. Two figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size are called similar figures.
2. All the congruent figures are similar but the converse is not true.
3. Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (i.e., proportion).
4. If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, then the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
5. If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
6. If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio and hence the two triangles are similar (AAA similarity criterion).
7. If in two triangles, two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to the two angles of the other triangle, then the two triangles are similar (AA similarity criterion).
8. If in two triangles, corresponding sides are in the same ratio, then their corresponding angles are equal and hence the triangles are similar (SSS similarity criterion).
9. If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and the sides including these angles are in the same ratio (proportional), then the triangles are similar (SAS similarity criterion).

content.text:
If in two right triangles, hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are proportional to the hypotenuse and one side of the other triangle, then the two triangles are similar. This may be referred to as the RHS Similarity Criterion.
If you use this criterion, some proofs you meet later will become simpler.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Recall the nine key results of the chapter: the definition of similar figures, two polygon similarity conditions, BPT, Converse BPT, AAA similarity criterion, AA corollary, SSS similarity criterion, SAS similarity criterion, and the RHS similarity criterion.

Distinguish the SAS and SSS similarity criteria from the corresponding SAS and SSS congruency criteria from Class IX by identifying the essential difference: proportional sides in similarity versus equal sides in congruency, with angle conditions preserved in both cases.

objectives.objective_text: Distinguish between congruent and similar figures by comparing their respective properties of shape and size.
Identify examples of similar figures in real-world contexts such as photographs of the same subject printed at different sizes.
State the two conditions required for two polygons of the same number of sides to be similar.
Verify whether two given polygons are similar by checking equality of corresponding angles and proportionality of corresponding sides.
Apply the definition of similar figures to classify given shapes and complete fill-in-the-blank and identification tasks.
Explain the proportional relationship that emerges when a line parallel to one side of a triangle intersects the other two sides, using the observations from the parallel-line construction activity.
Prove the Basic Proportionality Theorem using the areas of triangles ADE, BDE, and DEC formed by the parallel transversal line.
Prove the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem by an indirect argument showing that assuming DE is not parallel to BC leads to E and E' coinciding.
Apply the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its converse to prove proportionality results and identify isosceles triangles in multi-step geometric problems.
Apply BPT and its converse to find unknown lengths and verify whether lines are parallel in numerical problems.
Construct geometric proofs using BPT for problems involving trapezoids, mid-points, and intersecting diagonals.
Analyse multi-figure configurations to determine which form of BPT applies to each geometric situation.
Interpret the similarity notation △ABC ~ △DEF and correctly identify vertex correspondences for a pair of similar triangles.
Apply the AAA similarity criterion and its AA corollary to determine whether two triangles are similar given angle information.
Prove the SSS similarity criterion by constructing an auxiliary triangle congruent to the smaller triangle and applying BPT to establish angle equality.
Prove the SAS similarity criterion and distinguish it from the SAS congruency criterion by identifying the differing condition.
Apply AAA, SSS, and SAS similarity criteria to identify similar triangle pairs and find unknown angles or side ratios in geometric figures.
Solve real-world indirect measurement problems involving heights and shadows using the AA similarity criterion for triangles.
Translate a real-world geometric scenario into a similar triangle relationship and calculate unknown lengths through proportionality.

Apply SAS similarity to prove △AMC ∼ △PNR using the median-derived proportionality AM/PN = CA/RP and the included angle equality ∠MAC = ∠NPR, then chain the result to prove CM/RN = AB/PQ and to apply SSS similarity to prove △CMB ∼ △RNQ.
Identify similar triangle pairs in a figure of six triangle pairs and state the correct similarity criterion (AA, SSS, or SAS) with the symbolic similarity statement in correct vertex correspondence.

Construct multi-step geometric proofs using AAA, SSS, and SAS similarity criteria for configurations involving trapezoids with parallel sides, altitude intersections, isosceles triangles, and proportional medians.
Solve indirect-measurement problems involving poles and shadows and prove median proportionality in similar triangles using triangle similarity.

Recall the nine key results of the chapter: the definition of similar figures, two polygon similarity conditions, BPT, Converse BPT, AAA similarity criterion, AA corollary, SSS similarity criterion, SAS similarity criterion, and the RHS similarity criterion.

Distinguish the SAS and SSS similarity criteria from the corresponding SAS and SSS congruency criteria from Class IX by identifying the essential difference: proportional sides in similarity versus equal sides in congruency, with angle conditions preserved in both cases.

object.title: Similar vs Congruent Sorter
object.description: A sorting board. Pairs of figures are dragged into bins - 'congruent' (same shape and size) or 'similar but not congruent' (same shape, different size); feedback shows that similar figures relax the size requirement of congruence.
object.teaching_notes: Use when introducing similarity. Watch whether students see all congruent figures are similar but not vice versa. Follow up: are two squares always similar?
object.generation_prompt: A practice-mode matching tool for Grade 10 Maths distinguishing similar from congruent. UI: figure-pair cards and two bins; the student drags each, and feedback compares shape and size. Palette: violet bins, navy labels, green for correct sorting.
object.instructions_for_student: Sort each pair into 'congruent' or 'similar but not congruent' by comparing shape and size.

object.title: Polygon Similarity Tester
object.description: A similarity checker. Two polygons with the same number of sides are shown with their angles and side lengths; the student checks that corresponding angles are equal AND corresponding sides are in the same ratio, then decides whether they are similar.
object.teaching_notes: Use after the similarity definition. Insist BOTH conditions hold - equal angles and proportional sides. Follow up: are these two rectangles similar?
object.generation_prompt: A practice-mode calculation tool for Grade 10 Maths on polygon similarity. UI: two polygons with measures, inputs for the side ratios and angle checks, and a similar/not choice; on submit both conditions are tested. Palette: violet polygons, navy measures, green for correct answers.
object.instructions_for_student: Check that corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides share the same ratio, then decide whether the polygons are similar.

object.title: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales) Explorer
object.description: An interactive triangle. The student draws a line DE parallel to side BC of triangle ABC and drags it; the tool measures AD/DB and AE/EC and shows the two ratios stay equal, illustrating the Basic Proportionality Theorem.
object.teaching_notes: Use to discover the BPT through Activity 2. Ask what happens to the ratios as the parallel line moves. Follow up: if AD/DB = 2/3, what is AE/EC?
object.generation_prompt: A learn-mode geometry tool for Grade 10 Maths on the BPT. UI: a triangle with a draggable line parallel to BC; the ratios AD/DB and AE/EC are measured live and shown equal. Palette: violet triangle, navy ratio labels, soft grey background.
object.instructions_for_student: Draw a line parallel to BC and slide it. Watch the ratios AD/DB and AE/EC stay equal.

object.title: Trapezium Diagonal Theorem Visualizer
object.description: An interactive trapezium tool. In a trapezium with parallel sides, the diagonals intersect, and the tool shows the BPT applied to the triangles formed - the segments of the diagonals are in proportion. The student drags vertices to test it.
object.teaching_notes: Use with Exercise 6.2. Ask which triangles the diagonals create. Follow up: how do the diagonal segments relate in a trapezium?
object.generation_prompt: A learn-and-practice geometry tool for Grade 10 Maths applying the BPT in a trapezium. UI: a trapezium with both diagonals drawn and the proportional segments measured; dragging the vertices keeps the ratios equal. Palette: violet diagonals, navy ratio labels, soft grey background.
object.instructions_for_student: Draw the diagonals of the trapezium and watch the segment ratios stay equal by the BPT. Drag the vertices to test it.

object.title: AAA / AA Similarity Demonstrator
object.description: An interactive angle-matching tool. The student sets two angles of one triangle equal to two of another; the tool shows the third angles match too and that the corresponding sides come out in the same ratio, demonstrating AA (AAA) similarity.
object.teaching_notes: Use after Theorem 6.3. Ask why matching two angles is enough. Follow up: are two triangles with angles 50°, 60° similar?
object.generation_prompt: A learn-mode geometry tool for Grade 10 Maths on AAA/AA similarity. UI: two triangles with adjustable angles; matching two angles makes the third match and the side ratios equalise, flagged as similar. Palette: violet triangles, navy angle labels, soft grey background.
object.instructions_for_student: Match two angles of the triangles and watch the third match and the side ratios become equal - the triangles are similar.

object.title: SSS Similarity Verifier
object.description: A ratio-checking tool. Two triangles' three pairs of sides are given; the student computes the three ratios and decides whether they are all equal - if so the triangles are similar by SSS, and their angles must be equal.
object.teaching_notes: Use after Theorem 6.4. Insist students check ALL three ratios. Follow up: are triangles with sides 3,4,5 and 6,8,10 similar?
object.generation_prompt: A practice-mode calculation tool for Grade 10 Maths on SSS similarity. UI: two triangles with side lengths, inputs for the three side ratios, and a similar/not choice; on submit the ratios are compared. Palette: violet triangles, navy numbers, green for correct answers.
object.instructions_for_student: Work out the three pairs of side ratios and decide whether they are all equal - if so, the triangles are similar by SSS.

object.title: SAS Similarity Tester (included angle)
object.description: An included-angle checker. Two triangles are shown with one pair of equal angles and the two sides including that angle; the student checks those sides are in the same ratio and decides whether the triangles are similar by SAS.
object.teaching_notes: Use after Theorem 6.5. Insist the equal angle is the INCLUDED angle. Follow up: do the two sides about the equal angle share a ratio?
object.generation_prompt: A practice-mode calculation tool for Grade 10 Maths on SAS similarity. UI: two triangles with one marked equal angle and the including sides, inputs for the side ratio, and a similar/not choice; on submit the included-angle condition is checked. Palette: violet triangles, navy measures, green for correct answers.
object.instructions_for_student: Check that the angle is equal AND the two sides including it share the same ratio, then decide whether the triangles are similar by SAS.

object.title: Indirect Measurement Tool (lamp-post / shadow / Everest)
object.description: A real-world similarity solver. A height-and-shadow situation (a girl walking from a lamp-post, or a tall object and its shadow) forms two similar triangles; the student sets up the proportion of corresponding sides and solves for the unknown length.
object.teaching_notes: Use to apply AA similarity to measuring heights. At the predict step, check students match corresponding sides. Follow up: find the shadow length in the lamp-post problem.

object.instructions_for_student: Identify the two similar triangles, set up the proportion of corresponding sides, and solve for the unknown. Predict the proportion first.

object.title: Exercise 6.1 Strategy Walkthrough
object.description: A 2D animated strategy video for Exercise 6.1. An animated scene shows circles of different sizes morphing together with the text 'similar' highlighted in Orange. A second scene shows an equilateral triangle (three 60° angles) beside an isosceles triangle with apex angle 100°, with a side-by-side angle comparison: the 60°-60°-60° arcs remain consistent for all equilateral triangles while the isosceles apex angle changes. A third scene shows two example pairs annotated as similar and non-similar with brief text labels. A final scene displays the two quadrilaterals from Fig. 6.8 with a two-step check: angle check first (arcs appear one by one), then side-ratio check (ratio computations animate). The verdict 'similar' or 'not similar' appears at the end.
object.teaching_notes:
WHEN: Play this video AFTER students have attempted Exercise 6.1 independently on paper, so it serves as a solution reveal and strategy model - not a replacement for the attempt.
WHAT TO PAUSE AT: (1) Pause at approximately 80s (end of Scene 2, before the Fig. 6.8 check begins) and ask: 'What are the two steps you would use to check whether the quadrilaterals in Fig. 6.8 are similar? Write them before the video shows the answer.' This is the attempt-before-reveal moment. (2) Pause after Step 1 of Scene 3 (approx. 105s) and ask: 'Angles all match - is that enough to conclude similarity?'
WHAT TO ASK: After the video, ask: 'In Q1(iii), why is the answer equilateral and not isosceles? What property of equilateral triangles makes them all similar?' Encourage students to articulate the equal-angles reasoning.

carried_over_topics.summary: Similarity relaxes the congruence condition: two figures are similar when they have the same shape, regardless of size. All circles are similar, all squares are similar, and all equilateral triangles are similar, because within each family the shape is fixed regardless of the scale. The general rule follows: all congruent figures are similar, but similar figures need not be congruent. This concept applies directly when determining whether photographs printed at different sizes, or map-scale reductions of real regions, preserve the original shape faithfully.
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: Similar figures are defined as figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size, distinguishing them from congruent figures by relaxing the size requirement.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: How do cartographers compress an entire country onto a single sheet of paper while preserving its recognisable shape? How does a photographer enlarge a tiny 35 mm film negative into a poster-size print without distorting the image? The answer lies in a geometric concept called similarity.

RECALL: From Class IX, you know that two figures are congruent if they have the same shape and the same size. When you place one congruent figure exactly on top of another, every point coincides perfectly, leaving no gap or overlap.

CORE: Two figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size are called similar figures. Similarity relaxes the size requirement: only shape must be preserved.

Consider a concrete illustration: a 3 cm × 4 cm passport photograph and its 9 cm × 12 cm poster-size enlargement are similar figures. Every measurement in the poster is exactly three times the corresponding measurement in the passport photo, so shape is perfectly preserved while only scale has changed. A Survey of India topographic map of a 50 km stretch of the Ganga plains, plotted on a 10 cm grid at a fixed scale, works by the same principle - the shape of the region is preserved; only the size is reduced.

Three foundational facts:
• All circles are similar to one another. Every circle has the same shape - a closed round curve - regardless of its radius.
• All squares are similar to one another. Every square has four right angles and four equal sides, regardless of side length.
• All equilateral triangles are similar to one another. Every equilateral triangle has three 60° angles, regardless of size.

From these observations, a general rule follows: all congruent figures are similar, because if two figures match in both shape and size, they certainly match in shape alone. However, similar figures need not be congruent - the poster and the passport photograph are similar in shape, but they differ in size and are therefore not congruent.

ERROR ALERT: It is tempting to assume that any two figures of the same category - two rectangles, two isosceles triangles - are always similar. For circles, squares, and equilateral triangles this happens to be true. For other shapes it is not. A 1 × 2 rectangle and a 1 × 4 rectangle are both rectangles, yet they do not have the same shape. The formal conditions for similarity are developed in the next topic.

Can a circle and a square be similar? Can a triangle and a square be similar? A careful look at these figures confirms the answer is no: similarity requires the same shape, and fundamentally different shape types cannot be similar.

CHECK: Are all isosceles triangles similar to each other? Consider two isosceles triangles - one with apex angle 40° and another with apex angle 90°. Do they have the same shape? What does your answer tell you about when triangles of the same type are, or are not, similar?
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
You are familiar with triangles and many of their properties from your earlier classes. In Class IX, you have studied congruence of triangles in detail. Recall that two figures are said to be congruent, if they have the same shape and the same size. In this chapter, we shall study about those figures which have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Two figures having the same shape (and not necessarily the same size) are called similar figures. In particular, we shall discuss the similarity of triangles and apply this knowledge in giving a simple proof of Pythagoras Theorem learnt earlier.
Can you guess how heights of mountains (say Mount Everest) or distances of some long distant objects (say moon) have been found out? Do you think these have been measured directly with the help of a measuring tape? In fact, all these heights and distances have been found out using the idea of indirect measurements, which is based on the principle of similarity of figures (see Example 7, Q.15 of Exercise 6.3 and also Chapters 8 and 9 of this book).

6.2 Similar Figures
In Class IX, you have seen that all circles with the same radii are congruent, all squares with the same side lengths are congruent and all equilateral triangles with the same side lengths are congruent.
Now consider any two (or more) circles [see Fig. 6.1 (i)]. Are they congruent? Since all of them do not have the same radius, they are not congruent to each other. Note that some are congruent and some are not, but all of them have the same shape. So they all are, what we call, similar. Two similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Therefore, all circles are similar. What about two (or more) squares or two (or more) equilateral triangles [see Fig. 6.1 (ii) and (iii)]? As observed in the case of circles, here also all squares are similar and all equilateral triangles are similar.
From the above, we can say that all congruent figures are similar but the similar figures need not be congruent.
Can a circle and a square be similar? Can a triangle and a square be similar? These questions can be answered by just looking at the figures (see Fig. 6.1). Evidently these figures are not similar. (Why?)
concept_bullets: Two figures are similar when they share the same shape regardless of size - for example, a 3 cm × 4 cm passport photo and its 9 cm × 12 cm poster-size enlargement are similar because every dimension is scaled by the same factor of 3.
Congruent figures are always similar, but similar figures are not always congruent - for example, two equilateral triangles with sides 3 cm and 5 cm are similar but not congruent.
All circles are similar to one another regardless of radius - for example, a circle of radius 2 cm and a circle of radius 7 cm are similar because both are closed round curves with the same shape.

The general rule follows: all congruent figures are similar, but similar figures need not be congruent. This concept applies directly when determining whether photographs printed at different sizes, or map-scale reductions of real regions, preserve the original shape faithfully.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: In the previous topic, you established that similar figures share the same shape. Now you will develop the formal conditions that make this precise. When can you say, with certainty, that two given polygons are similar?

CORE - Two Conditions for Polygon Similarity:

Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar if and only if both of the following conditions hold simultaneously:
(i)  Their corresponding angles are equal, AND
(ii) Their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).

The common ratio of corresponding sides is called the scale factor (or Representative Fraction) for the pair of similar polygons. World maps and architectural blueprints are both prepared by selecting an appropriate scale factor and maintaining it consistently for all corresponding distances. A scale factor greater than 1 indicates an enlargement; a scale factor between 0 and 1 indicates a reduction; a scale factor of exactly 1 means the two polygons are congruent.

Activity 1 illustrates how this arises naturally. When a lighted bulb at point O on the ceiling casts a shadow of a cardboard quadrilateral ABCD onto a table below, the shadow A’B’C’D’ is an enlargement of ABCD. Because light travels in straight lines, vertex A’ lies on ray OA, vertex B’ lies on ray OB, vertex C’ lies on ray OC, and vertex D’ lies on ray OD. The four vertices of the shadow are therefore determined entirely by the four rays from the light source O through the four vertices of the original card. Measuring the shadow confirms:
(i)  ∠A = ∠A’, ∠B = ∠B’, ∠C = ∠C’, ∠D = ∠D’, and
(ii) AB/A’B’ = BC/B’C’ = CD/C’D’ = DA/D’A’.
Both conditions are satisfied; quadrilateral ABCD is therefore similar to quadrilateral A’B’C’D’. The common scale factor equals the ratio OA’/OA, which is the same for all four vertices because all four rays originate from the single point O.

WHY ARE ANGLES PRESERVED? When two sides of ABCD meeting at vertex A are extended along rays OA, OB, OC from point O, the two extended sides at A’ make the same angle with each other as the original sides at A. This is because angles are determined by the directions of two rays, and extending a ray from O does not change its direction. The shadow angle equals the original angle.

Photograph enlargement gives a further illustration. When a photographer enlarges a 35 mm negative to a 55 mm print, every line segment in the larger print is in the ratio 55:35 = 11:7 with the corresponding line segment in the smaller print. Simultaneously, the inclination (angle) between any pair of corresponding line segments is preserved by the optical enlargement process. This is precisely the essence of similarity - proportional sides and equal angles together. If only the size changed while one dimension stretched more than another, the photograph would appear distorted; the fact that it does not is exactly because both similarity conditions hold.

Notation: When polygon P₁ is similar to polygon P₂, we write P₁ ∼ P₂. The symbol ‘∼’ stands for ‘is similar to’, in contrast to ‘≅’ which stands for ‘is congruent to’. Crucially, the vertices must be listed in the order of their correspondence. If quadrilateral ABCD ∼ quadrilateral A’B’C’D’, then A corresponds to A’, B to B’, C to C’, and D to D’. Writing the correspondence out of order - for example, ABCD ∼ B’A’C’D’ - is incorrect unless the correspondence actually holds in that order. From the correspondence ABCD ∼ A’B’C’D’, you can immediately read off both conditions: angles ∠A = ∠A’, ∠B = ∠B’, ∠C = ∠C’, ∠D = ∠D’, and ratios AB/A’B’ = BC/B’C’ = CD/C’D’ = DA/D’A’ = k, where k is the scale factor.

WHY BOTH CONDITIONS? - Three Counter-Examples:

Counter-example 1 (Fig. 6.6): A square and a rectangle. All four corresponding angles are 90°, so condition (i) is satisfied. However, for a 2 × 2 square and a 2 × 4 rectangle, one pair of sides has ratio 2/2 = 1 and the other has ratio 2/4 = 1/2. The ratios are not equal, so condition (ii) fails. These two quadrilaterals are NOT similar despite having equal angles. The rectangle looks ‘stretched’ in one direction compared to the square, confirming that shape has changed.

Counter-example 2 (Fig. 6.7): A square and a rhombus. If the square has side a and the rhombus has side a as well, every corresponding side ratio equals 1, so condition (ii) is satisfied. However, the square has four 90° angles, whereas the rhombus (unless it is itself a square) has two acute and two obtuse angles. Condition (i) fails. These two quadrilaterals are NOT similar despite having proportional sides. The rhombus looks ‘tilted’ or ‘squashed’ compared to the square, confirming again that equal side ratios alone cannot capture the same shape.

Counter-example 3 (the Jaipur tiles context): At a marble showroom in Jaipur, a designer compares two rhombus-shaped floor tiles available in different sizes. Both tiles have a 60° acute angle, so all four pairs of corresponding angles are equal - condition (i) holds for the pair. However, a careful measurement of the diagonals reveals that the ratio of the longer diagonal to the shorter diagonal is different for the two tiles, which means their corresponding sides are not in the same ratio. Condition (ii) fails. The two tiles are therefore not similar, even though they belong to the same shape category and share the same angle. This confirms that angle equality alone is insufficient for polygon similarity of any kind.

Remark on Transitivity: If polygon P₁ is similar to polygon P₂, and P₂ is similar to polygon P₃, then P₁ is similar to P₃. Similarity is a transitive relation among polygons with the same number of sides. Transitivity is useful when a proof proceeds in two steps: first establishing that figure X is similar to figure Y, then establishing that figure Y is similar to figure Z, and concluding that X is similar to Z without needing a direct comparison between X and Z.

A USEFUL CONSEQUENCE - Perimeters of Similar Polygons: If two polygons are similar with scale factor k, then the ratio of their perimeters equals k as well. This is because each side of the larger polygon is k times the corresponding side of the smaller polygon, so the sum of all sides (the perimeter) is also k times the smaller perimeter. The areas of similar figures, however, are in the ratio k² - this will be explored in later work on areas of similar triangles.

ERROR ALERT: Both the square-rectangle and square-rhombus counter-examples demonstrate the same important point from opposite directions: neither equal angles alone nor proportional sides alone is sufficient to guarantee similarity of two polygons. The only reliable test is to verify both conditions together. Students often assume that ‘same shape’ is intuitively obvious, but the counter-examples show that your geometric intuition must be backed by an explicit check of both conditions.

CHECK: Quadrilateral ABCD is a square with side 3 cm. Quadrilateral PQRS is a square with side 5 cm. Verify that both similarity conditions hold and confirm that ABCD ∼ PQRS with scale factor 5/3. Then consider: quadrilateral WXYZ is a rectangle with sides 3 cm and 5 cm. Is ABCD ∼ WXYZ? Check condition (ii) specifically by computing the ratio of each pair of corresponding sides and determine whether the ratios are equal.
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
What can you say about the two quadrilaterals ABCD and PQRS (see Fig 6.2)? Are they similar? These figures appear to be similar but we cannot be certain about it. Therefore, we must have some definition of similarity of figures and based on this definition some rules to decide whether the two given figures are similar or not. For this, let us look at the photographs given in Fig. 6.3:
You will at once say that they are the photographs of the same monument (Taj Mahal) but are in different sizes. Would you say that the three photographs are similar? Yes, they are.
What can you say about the two photographs of the same size of the same person one at the age of 10 years and the other at the age of 40 years? Are these photographs similar? These photographs are of the same size but certainly they are not of the same shape. So, they are not similar.
What does the photographer do when she prints photographs of different sizes from the same negative? You must have heard about the stamp size, passport size and postcard size photographs. She generally takes a photograph on a small size film, say of 35mm size and then enlarges it into a bigger size, say 45mm (or 55mm). Thus, if we consider any line segment in the smaller photograph (figure), its corresponding line segment in the bigger photograph (figure) will be 45/35 or 55/35 of that of the line segment. This really means that every line segment of the smaller photograph is enlarged (increased) in the ratio 35:45 (or 35:55). It can also be said that every line segment of the bigger photograph is reduced (decreased) in the ratio 45:35 (or 55:35). Further, if you consider inclinations (or angles) between any pair of corresponding line segments in the two photographs of different sizes, you shall see that these inclinations (or angles) are always equal. This is the essence of the similarity of two figures and in particular of two polygons. We say that:
Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).
Note that the same ratio of the corresponding sides is referred to as the scale factor (or the Representative Fraction) for the polygons. You must have heard that world maps (i.e., global maps) and blue prints for the construction of a building are prepared using a suitable scale factor and observing certain conventions.
In order to understand similarity of figures more clearly, let us perform the following activity:
Activity 1 : Place a lighted bulb at a point O on the ceiling and directly below it a table in your classroom. Let us cut a polygon, say a quadrilateral ABCD, from a plane cardboard and place this cardboard parallel to the ground between the lighted bulb and the table. Then a shadow of ABCD is cast on the table. Mark the outline of this shadow as A'B'C'D' (see Fig.6.4).
Note that the quadrilateral A'B'C'D' is an enlargement (or magnification) of the quadrilateral ABCD. This is because of the property of light that light propagates in a straight line. You may also note that A' lies on ray OA, B' lies on ray OB, C' lies on OC and D' lies on OD. Thus, quadrilaterals ABCD and A'B'C'D' are of the same shape but of different sizes.
So, quadrilateral ABCD is similar to quadrilateral A'B'C'D'. We can also say that quadrilateral A'B'C'D' is similar to the quadrilateral ABCD.
Here, you can also note that vertex A corresponds to vertex A', vertex B corresponds to vertex B', vertex C corresponds to vertex C' and vertex D corresponds to vertex D'. Symbolically, these correspondences are represented as A↔A', B↔B', C↔C' and D↔D'. By actually measuring the angles and the sides of the two quadrilaterals, you may verify that
(i) ∠A = ∠A', ∠B = ∠B', ∠C = ∠C', ∠D = ∠D' and
(ii) AB/A'B' = BC/B'C' = CD/C'D' = DA/D'A'.
This again emphasises that two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) all the corresponding angles are equal and (ii) all the corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).
From the above, you can easily say that quadrilaterals ABCD and PQRS of Fig. 6.5 are similar.
Remark : You can verify that if one polygon is similar to another polygon and this second polygon is similar to a third polygon, then the first polygon is similar to the third polygon.
You may note that in the two quadrilaterals (a square and a rectangle) of Fig. 6.6, corresponding angles are equal, but their corresponding sides are not in the same ratio. So, the two quadrilaterals are not similar. Similarly, you may note that in the two quadrilaterals (a square and a rhombus) of Fig. 6.7, corresponding sides are in the same ratio, but their corresponding angles are not equal. Again, the two polygons (quadrilaterals) are not similar.
Thus, either of the above two conditions (i) and (ii) of similarity of two polygons is not sufficient for them to be similar.
concept_bullets: Two polygons are similar only when both conditions hold together - for example, a 2 × 2 square and a 2 × 4 rectangle have all right angles equal (condition i satisfied) but side ratios 2/2 = 1 and 2/4 = 1/2 are unequal (condition ii fails), so they are not similar.
The scale factor k is the common ratio of every corresponding side pair - for example, if ABCD ∼ A'B'C'D' with k = 3, then each side of A'B'C'D' is exactly 3 times the corresponding side of ABCD.
A scale factor of exactly 1 means the two similar polygons are congruent - for example, two squares each of side 4 cm are both similar (same shape) and congruent (same size) with k = 1.
Similarity is a transitive relation: if polygon P₁ ∼ P₂ and P₂ ∼ P₃, then P₁ ∼ P₃, useful when a proof proceeds in two steps through an intermediate figure.

recall_questions.prompt: State the two conditions that must hold simultaneously for two polygons of the same number of sides to be called similar.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: ABCD is a square with side 4 cm; PQRS is a square with side 6 cm.

Condition (i) - Corresponding angles: Every square has four right angles (90°). So ∠A = ∠P = ∠B = ∠Q = ∠C = ∠R = ∠D = ∠S = 90°. All four pairs of corresponding angles are equal. ✓

Condition (ii) - Corresponding sides in the same ratio:
AB/PQ = 4/6 = 2/3
BC/QR = 4/6 = 2/3
CD/RS = 4/6 = 2/3
DA/SP = 4/6 = 2/3
All four ratios are equal. ✓

Since both conditions hold, ABCD ∼ PQRS. Scale factor = 2/3.
recall_questions.prompt: Quadrilateral ABCD is a square with side 4 cm. Quadrilateral PQRS is a square with side 6 cm. Verify that ABCD ∼ PQRS by checking both similarity conditions, and state the scale factor.

recall_questions.answer:
The student is incorrect. Condition (ii) - proportional sides - does hold: all four sides of the square are 3 cm and all four sides of the rhombus are 3 cm, so every corresponding side ratio is 3/3 = 1. ✓

However, condition (i) - equal corresponding angles - fails. The square has all angles 90°. The rhombus has two angles of 60° and two angles of 120°. The corresponding angles are not equal: 90° ≠ 60° and 90° ≠ 120°. ✗

Since condition (i) fails, the two quadrilaterals are NOT similar. Both conditions must hold simultaneously; satisfying only one is not sufficient.
recall_questions.prompt: A 3 cm × 3 cm square ABCD and a rhombus PQRS with side 3 cm and angles 60° and 120° are compared. A student says they are similar because all corresponding sides have ratio 1. Is this correct? Show clearly which condition fails.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
STRATEGY OVERVIEW: Exercise 6.1 consolidates your understanding of the two foundational ideas from this segment - the definition of similar figures (Topic 1) and the two formal conditions for polygon similarity (Topic 2). Work through each question in order, since each one targets a specific part of these concepts.

Question 1 - Fill in the Blanks (Recall of Core Facts):
This question tests whether you can correctly distinguish between ‘similar’ and ‘congruent’. Before attempting it, review the following:
• All circles are similar (same shape regardless of radius).
• All squares are similar (same shape regardless of side length).
• All equilateral triangles are similar (three 60° angles regardless of size).
• The two conditions: polygons are similar when (a) corresponding angles are equal AND (b) corresponding sides are proportional.

WORKED EXAMPLE MODEL (for part (iii)):
The blank reads: “All ___ triangles are similar. (isosceles, equilateral)”
Step 1: Ask - are all isosceles triangles the same shape? An isosceles triangle can have any apex angle from just above 0° to just below 180°. Two isosceles triangles with apex angles of 40° and 100° do not have the same shape, so they are not similar.
Step 2: Ask - are all equilateral triangles the same shape? Every equilateral triangle has three angles of exactly 60°. No matter the side length, the shape is always the same.
Conclusion: All equilateral triangles are similar. The answer is equilateral.

Question 2 - Give Two Examples Each (Creative Recall):
For similar figures: think of everyday objects that come in different sizes but preserve shape - two photographs printed from the same negative at different sizes, two coins of the same denomination from different years (same shape, possibly different size), or two national flags of different dimensions.
For non-similar figures: think of objects that look superficially alike but differ in shape - a square versus a rectangle with different proportions, or an equilateral triangle versus a right-angled triangle.

Question 3 - State Whether Quadrilaterals Are Similar (Application of Both Conditions):
Look at Fig. 6.8 and apply the two-condition test systematically:
Step 1: Check whether all corresponding angles are equal. Measure or use the given angle information.
Step 2: Check whether all corresponding sides are in the same ratio. Calculate the ratios of corresponding sides.
Only if both steps confirm the conditions should you conclude that the quadrilaterals are similar.

ERROR ALERT: Do not judge similarity by appearance alone. A quadrilateral can look similar to another and yet fail one of the two conditions when you check numerically. Always verify both conditions before stating your conclusion.
