concept_bullets: All equilateral triangles are similar regardless of side length because every equilateral triangle has three 60° angles - for example, an equilateral triangle of side 2 cm and one of side 9 cm are similar with scale factor 9/2.

To classify two quadrilaterals as similar or not, both conditions must be checked - for example, two quadrilaterals may look alike yet fail condition (ii) if their side ratios are 1/2 and 1/3 rather than a uniform ratio.
Non-similar figures of the same category exist - for example, a 1 × 3 rectangle and a 1 × 5 rectangle are both rectangles but not similar because the side ratios 1/1 = 1 and 3/5 ≠ 1 are unequal.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: Exercise 6.1 consolidates the two foundational concepts of Segment 1 through direct application tasks. The fill-in-the-blank items require correct recall of which standard figure families are always similar and which conditions polygon similarity demands. The example-giving task requires creative retrieval: students must produce both a similar pair and a non-similar pair from everyday contexts. The quadrilateral classification task requires applying the two-condition test systematically to Fig. 6.8, verifying angle equality and side-ratio equality before stating a conclusion. Students practise the discipline of not judging similarity by appearance alone.
important_points: All circles are ___. (congruent, similar)
All squares are ___. (similar, congruent)
All ___ triangles are similar. (isosceles, equilateral)
Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (a) their corresponding angles are ___ and (b) their corresponding sides are ___. (equal, proportional)

recall_questions.answer:
Equilateral triangles are always similar to each other, because every equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°, so any two equilateral triangles have equal corresponding angles regardless of size.

Isosceles triangles are NOT always similar. An isosceles triangle can have any apex angle from just above 0° to just below 180°. For example, an isosceles triangle with apex angle 40° and an isosceles triangle with apex angle 100° have different angle sets, so they do not have the same shape and are not similar.
recall_questions.prompt: In Exercise 6.1, which class of triangles are always similar to each other - isosceles or equilateral? Explain why the other class is not always similar.

recall_questions.answer: The student has skipped checking condition (ii): that all four pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio. As the square-and-rectangle counter-example in Topic T2 shows, two quadrilaterals can have all four corresponding angles equal (all 90°) and yet have different side ratios - for instance, a 2 × 2 square and a 2 × 4 rectangle. In that case they are NOT similar despite equal angles. Both conditions must be checked before concluding similarity; equal angles alone is not sufficient for polygons.

The ancient Greek mathematician Thales first identified the proportionality property of equiangular triangles, and the theorem named after him formalises the activity observation. carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: You have established that two polygons are similar when their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in the same ratio. Since a triangle is also a polygon, these two conditions apply to triangles as well.

Two triangles are similar if:
(i)  their corresponding angles are equal, and
(ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).

CORE - Equiangular Triangles and Thales’ Theorem:
When two triangles have all three pairs of corresponding angles equal, they are called equiangular triangles. The ancient Greek mathematician Thales discovered an important result about equiangular triangles: the ratio of any two corresponding sides in two equiangular triangles is always the same. It is believed that Thales used what is now called the Basic Proportionality Theorem (also known as Thales’ Theorem) to establish this.

Activity 2 introduces the theorem through a direct construction. Draw any angle XAY. On arm AX, mark five equally spaced points P, Q, D, R, and B such that AP = PQ = QD = DR = RB. Through B, draw any line intersecting arm AY at C (see Fig. 6.9). Through point D, draw a line parallel to BC, intersecting AC at E.

From the construction, you can observe that AD/DB = 3/2 (since AD spans three equal parts and DB spans two). Now measure AE and EC. Do you observe that AE/EC is also equal to 3/2? This is not a coincidence: in △ABC, the line DE is parallel to BC, and AD/DB = AE/EC.

A practical interpretation: a farmer in Vidarbha, Maharashtra, owns a triangular plot ABC with the road running along the base BC. To divide the plot with a fence line DE parallel to BC such that AD:DB = 2:3, the farmer only needs to place fence-post D on side AB with AD:DB = 2:3 and fence-post E on side AC with AE:EC = 2:3. The theorem guarantees that DE will then be parallel to BC automatically - no angle measurement at D or E is required. Only the ratios along the two sides need to match.

WHY THIS STEP? Activity 2 demonstrates this with one specific ratio (3:2). The same experiment can be repeated with any ratio - marking different numbers of equal parts on AX - and the result is the same every time: AD/DB = AE/EC whenever DE ∥ BC.

This relationship is the content of the Basic Proportionality Theorem, which is proved rigorously in the next topic.

CHECK: In Activity 2, if D were placed so that AD/DB = 4/1, what would you expect AE/EC to equal before measuring? If you now moved D to a new position where AD/DB = 1/4, would the line through D parallel to BC still intersect AY at a point E satisfying AE/EC = 1/4? How would you verify this?

6.3 Similarity of Triangles
What can you say about the similarity of two triangles?
You may recall that triangle is also a polygon. So, we can state the same conditions for the similarity of two triangles. That is:
Two triangles are similar, if
(i) their corresponding angles are equal and
(ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).
Note that if corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, then they are known as equiangular triangles. A famous Greek mathematician Thales gave an important truth relating to two equiangular triangles which is as follows:
The ratio of any two corresponding sides in two equiangular triangles is always the same.
It is believed that he had used a result called the Basic Proportionality Theorem (now known as the Thales Theorem) for the same.
To understand the Basic Proportionality Theorem, let us perform the following activity:
Activity 2 : Draw any angle XAY and on its one arm AX, mark points (say five points) P, Q, D, R and B such that AP = PQ = QD = DR = RB.
Now, through B, draw any line intersecting arm AY at C (see Fig. 6.9).
Also, through the point D, draw a line parallel to BC to intersect AC at E. Do you observe from your constructions that AD/DB = 3/2? Measure AE and EC. What about AE/EC? Observe that AE/EC is also equal to 3/2. Thus, you can see that in △ABC, DE ∥ BC and AD/DB = AE/EC. Is it a coincidence? No, it is due to the following theorem (known as the Basic Proportionality Theorem):
concept_bullets: When a line is drawn through a point D on AB parallel to BC, it automatically divides AC in exactly the same ratio as it divides AB - for example, if AD/DB = 2/3, then AE/EC = 2/3 regardless of the size of △ABC.
Equiangular triangles always have proportional corresponding sides - for example, two triangles both with angles 60°, 70°, 50° will have all three side ratios equal even if their sizes differ.
Thales' result applies to any ratio: marking AD/DB = 4/1 and drawing DE parallel to BC forces AE/EC = 4/1, confirming the proportionality holds universally.

recall_questions.answer: The Basic Proportionality Theorem states: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio. That is, in △ABC, if DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC, then AD/DB = AE/EC.
recall_questions.prompt: State what the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales' Theorem) says about a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle.

recall_questions.answer:
Activity 2 demonstrated this through direct measurement: when D was placed so that AD/DB = 3/2 and a line DE was drawn through D parallel to BC, measuring AE and EC showed AE/EC was also exactly 3/2. Repeating the activity with different ratios always gave the same result: the ratio on the first side (AD/DB) exactly equalled the ratio on the second side (AE/EC).

The reason is that the parallel line DE 'copies' the same proportional division onto both sides simultaneously. Since DE cuts both sides AB and AC in a consistent way (anchored by the parallel condition), both sides end up divided in the same ratio. This observation is the content of the Basic Proportionality Theorem.
recall_questions.prompt: In △ABC, line DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. Explain why Activity 2 demonstrated that AD/DB must equal AE/EC.

recall_questions.answer:
If AD/DB = 4/1, then by the Basic Proportionality Theorem, AE/EC = 4/1 as well.

The theorem guarantees this because the theorem states that whenever DE ∥ BC in △ABC, both sides AB and AC are divided in the same ratio by the line DE. The ratio AD/DB is determined by the position of D on AB. Once D is fixed and DE is drawn parallel to BC, there is exactly one point E on AC where the parallel line meets it. The theorem asserts that for this unique E, the ratio AE/EC must equal AD/DB - no measurement is needed because the parallel condition forces the equality. Activity 2 confirms this by experiment, and the formal proof in the next topic establishes it with certainty.
recall_questions.prompt: In Activity 2, if AD/DB = 4/1, what would you expect AE/EC to equal before measuring? Explain why the theorem guarantees this without needing to measure.

carried_over_topics.summary: Theorem 6.1 states that if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio. The proof constructs auxiliary diagonals BE and CD and perpendiculars EN ⊥ AB and DM ⊥ AC to express four area ratios. Triangles ADE and BDE share height EN, giving ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB. Triangles ADE and DEC share height DM, giving ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC. Because triangles BDE and DEC share the same base DE and lie between the same parallel lines BC and DE, their areas are equal. Combining the three equations yields AD/DB = AE/EC.
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: Theorem 6.1 (BPT) is proved using area ratios of triangles ADE, BDE, and DEC formed by auxiliary lines, establishing that DE parallel to BC implies AD/DB equals AE/EC.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
THEOREM STATEMENT:
Theorem 6.1: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.

GIVEN:
A triangle ABC in which a line DE, parallel to side BC, intersects sides AB and AC at points D and E respectively (see Fig. 6.10).

TO PROVE:
AD/DB = AE/EC

CONSTRUCTION:
Join BE and CD. Draw DM ⊥ AC and EN ⊥ AB.

PROOF STEPS:

(i) Express areas using the base-height formula:
    ar(ADE) = 1/2 × AD × EN
    ar(BDE) = 1/2 × DB × EN
    WHY? Both △ADE and △BDE share the same height EN (the perpendicular from E to line AB), but have different bases AD and DB along line AB.
    Therefore, ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = (AD × EN)/(DB × EN) = AD/DB ... (1)

(ii) Similarly:
    ar(ADE) = 1/2 × AE × DM
    ar(DEC) = 1/2 × EC × DM
    WHY? Both △ADE and △DEC share the same height DM (the perpendicular from D to line AC), but have different bases AE and EC along line AC.
    Therefore, ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = (AE × DM)/(EC × DM) = AE/EC ... (2)

(iii) Establish that ar(BDE) = ar(DEC):
    WHY? Triangles BDE and DEC share the same base DE and both lie between the same pair of parallel lines BC and DE.
    Therefore, ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) ... (3)

(iv) Combine equations (1), (2), and (3):
    From (1): ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB
    From (2): ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC
    From (3): ar(BDE) = ar(DEC)
    Since the denominators in (1) and (2) are equal, the left-hand sides of (1) and (2) are equal.
    Therefore, AD/DB = AE/EC.

CONCLUSION:
Hence, if DE ∥ BC, then AD/DB = AE/EC. □

ERROR ALERT: Step (iii) relies on the theorem that two triangles on the same base and between the same pair of parallel lines have equal areas. This result was proved in Class IX (Chapter 9). It is essential that DE ∥ BC for this step to hold - if DE is not parallel to BC, triangles BDE and DEC do not lie between the same parallels and their areas are not necessarily equal, so the proof breaks down.

CHECK: In the proof, why is it necessary to draw both auxiliaries - the join BE, the join CD, and the perpendiculars DM and EN? Could the proof work with just one perpendicular? Think about which area ratios each perpendicular is used to express.
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Theorem 6.1 : If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
Proof : We are given a triangle ABC in which a line parallel to side BC intersects other two sides AB and AC at D and E respectively (see Fig. 6.10).
We need to prove that AD/DB = AE/EC.
Let us join BE and CD and then draw DM ⊥ AC and EN ⊥ AB.
Now, area of △ADE (= 1/2 × base × height) = 1/2 × AD × EN.
Recall from Class IX, that area of △ADE is denoted as ar(ADE).
So, ar(ADE) = 1/2 × AD × EN
Similarly, ar(BDE) = 1/2 × DB × EN,
ar(ADE) = 1/2 × AE × DM and ar(DEC) = 1/2 × EC × DM.
Therefore, ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = (AD × EN)/(DB × EN) = AD/DB ... (1)
and ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = (AE × DM)/(EC × DM) = AE/EC ... (2)
Note that △BDE and DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels BC and DE.
So, ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) ... (3)
Therefore, from (1), (2) and (3), we have :
AD/DB = AE/EC
concept_bullets: The ratio AD/DB is obtained by comparing the areas of △ADE and △BDE, which share perpendicular height EN from E to line AB - for example, if AD = 3 cm and DB = 2 cm, then ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = 3/2.
Triangles BDE and DEC have equal areas because they share base DE and both lie between parallel lines BC and DE - this equal-area result is the key linking step that forces AD/DB = AE/EC.

The proof requires two separate perpendiculars (EN to AB and DM to AC) because each perpendicular enables a different area ratio, and only combining both ratios with the equal-area step yields the final result.

By the Class IX theorem that triangles on the same base and between the same parallel lines have equal areas, ar(BDE) = ar(DEC).

Step 1: ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = (½ × AD × EN)/(½ × DB × EN) = AD/DB ... (1)
[Both triangles share height EN from E to AB; bases are AD and DB.]

Step 2: ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = (½ × AE × DM)/(½ × EC × DM) = AE/EC ... (2)
[Both triangles share height DM from D to AC; bases are AE and EC.]

Step 3: Since DE ∥ BC, triangles BDE and DEC share base DE and lie between the same parallels, so ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) ... (3)

recall_questions.answer:
Error: The student has incorrectly formed the area ratios. ar(BDE)/ar(DEC) is not equal to BD/EC because BD and EC are not bases of these triangles for a shared height.

Correct relationships:
- ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB (shared height EN from E, bases AD and DB on AB).
- ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC (shared height DM from D, bases AE and EC on AC).
- Since ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) (same base DE, same parallels BC and DE), we combine these two equations: AD/DB = AE/EC.

The error is in choosing the wrong triangle pair and the wrong base-height combination when forming area ratios.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: Theorem 6.1 established that a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. The natural question is: does the converse also hold? If a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, must it necessarily be parallel to the third side?

Activity 3 investigates this. Draw angle XAY and mark five equally spaced points B₁, B₂, B₃, B₄, B on ray AX such that AB₁ = B₁B₂ = B₂B₃ = B₃B₄ = B₄B. Similarly, mark five equally spaced points C₁, C₂, C₃, C₄, C on ray AY with the same equal spacing. Join B₁C₁ and BC (see Fig. 6.11).

From the construction:
AB₁/B₁B = AC₁/C₁C = 1/4, and B₁C₁ ∥ BC ... (1)
AB₂/B₂B = AC₂/C₂C = 2/3, and B₂C₂ ∥ BC ... (2)
AB₃/B₃B = AC₃/C₃C = 3/2, and B₃C₃ ∥ BC ... (3)
AB₄/B₄B = AC₄/C₄C = 4/1, and B₄C₄ ∥ BC ... (4)

In every case, when two sides are divided in the same ratio, the joining line is parallel to the base. This leads to Theorem 6.2.

THEOREM STATEMENT:
Theorem 6.2: If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.

GIVEN:
A triangle ABC. A line DE intersects AB at D and AC at E such that AD/DB = AE/EC.

TO PROVE:
DE ∥ BC

PROOF STEPS:

(i) Suppose, for contradiction, that DE is not parallel to BC.

(ii) Construct the unique line DE’ through D such that DE’ ∥ BC (see Fig. 6.12).
    WHY? Through any point, exactly one line parallel to a given line can be drawn.

(iii) Apply Theorem 6.1 to △ABC with the parallel line DE’:
    AD/DB = AE’/E’C ... (*)
    WHY? Since DE’ ∥ BC, Theorem 6.1 guarantees this ratio equality.

(iv) We are given that AD/DB = AE/EC.
    From (*) and the given condition: AE/EC = AE’/E’C.

(v) Add 1 to both sides:
    AE/EC + 1 = AE’/E’C + 1
    (AE + EC)/EC = (AE’ + E’C)/E’C
    AC/EC = AC/E’C
    WHY? AE + EC = AC and AE’ + E’C = AC (both are the full length of side AC).
    Therefore, EC = E’C.
    WHY? If AC/EC = AC/E’C, then the denominators must be equal.

(vi) Since EC = E’C, points E and E’ coincide. Therefore DE and DE’ are the same line. But DE’ ∥ BC, so DE ∥ BC. This contradicts our assumption that DE is not parallel to BC.

CONCLUSION:
Hence, if AD/DB = AE/EC, then DE ∥ BC. □

ERROR ALERT: The ‘add 1 to both sides’ step is a standard algebraic manipulation that students sometimes find confusing in a geometric context. Recall that for any fraction a/b, adding 1 gives (a + b)/b. Here: AE/EC + 1 = (AE + EC)/EC = AC/EC. The key insight is that AE + EC equals the total length AC, which is the same for both sides of the equation. This step allows you to compare the full side AC against the segment EC on one side and E’C on the other, forcing them to be equal.

CHECK: In a triangle PQR, a line ST meets PQ at S and PR at T such that PS/SQ = PT/TR = 3/5. Without measuring, can you immediately conclude that ST ∥ QR? Which theorem justifies this conclusion, and what are the given condition and the conclusion in terms of this theorem?
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Is the converse of this theorem also true (For the meaning of converse, see Appendix 1)? To examine this, let us perform the following activity:
Activity 3 : Draw an angle XAY on your notebook and on ray AX, mark points B₁, B₂, B₃, B₄ and B such that AB₁ = B₁B₂ = B₂B₃ = B₃B₄ = B₄B.
Similarly, on ray AY, mark points C₁, C₂, C₃, C₄ and C such that AC₁ = C₁C₂ = C₂C₃ = C₃C₄ = C₄C. Then join B₁C₁ and BC (see Fig. 6.11).
Note that AB₁/B₁B = AC₁/C₁C = 1/4. You can also see that lines B₁C₁ and BC are parallel to each other, i.e., B₁C₁ ∥ BC ... (1)
Similarly, by joining B₂C₂, B₃C₃ and B₄C₄, you can see that:
AB₂/B₂B = AC₂/C₂C = 2/3 and B₂C₂ ∥ BC ... (2)
AB₃/B₃B = AC₃/C₃C = 3/2 and B₃C₃ ∥ BC ... (3)
AB₄/B₄B = AC₄/C₄C = 4/1 and B₄C₄ ∥ BC ... (4)
From (1), (2), (3) and (4), it can be observed that if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
You can repeat this activity by drawing any angle XAY of different measure and taking any number of equal parts on arms AX and AY. Each time, you will arrive at the same result. Thus, we obtain the following theorem, which is the converse of Theorem 6.1:

Theorem 6.2 : If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
This theorem can be proved by taking a line DE such that AD/DB = AE/EC and assuming that DE is not parallel to BC (see Fig. 6.12).
If DE is not parallel to BC, draw a line DE' parallel to BC.
So, AD/DB = AE'/E'C (Why?)
Therefore, AE/EC = AE'/E'C (Why?)
Adding 1 to both sides of above, you can see that E and E' must coincide. (Why?)
concept_bullets: If AD/DB = AE/EC in △ABC, then DE ∥ BC - for example, if AD/DB = 3/5 and AE/EC = 3/5, then the line through D and E is parallel to BC by Theorem 6.2.
The 'add 1 to both sides' step converts segment ratios into full-side ratios: AE/EC + 1 = (AE + EC)/EC = AC/EC, allowing direct comparison of AC/EC and AC/E'C to conclude EC = E'C.
Activity 3 confirms the converse for ratios 1/4, 2/3, 3/2, and 4/1 - in every case, the joining line B₁C₁ (or B₂C₂, etc.) is parallel to BC, providing empirical evidence before the formal proof.

Combined with the given AD/DB = AE/EC, this yields AE/EC = AE'/E'C. Adding 1 to both sides and simplifying with the fact that AE + EC = AE' + E'C = AC forces EC = E'C, making E and E' the same point. This contradicts the assumption that DE ≠ DE', completing the proof by contradiction.
important_points: Theorem 6.2 : If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
AD/DB = AE'/E'C (Why?)
AE/EC = AE'/E'C (Why?)

recall_questions.answer:
Theorem 6.2 (Converse BPT): If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.

Theorem 6.1 says: IF DE ∥ BC, THEN AD/DB = AE/EC. (Parallel line → equal ratios.)
Theorem 6.2 says: IF AD/DB = AE/EC, THEN DE ∥ BC. (Equal ratios → parallel line.)
The hypothesis and conclusion are exactly exchanged, making Theorem 6.2 the logical converse of Theorem 6.1.
recall_questions.prompt: State Theorem 6.2 (Converse of BPT). How is its hypothesis and conclusion the reverse of Theorem 6.1?

recall_questions.answer:
Given: PS/SQ = 3/5 and PT/TR = 3/5.

Since PS/SQ = PT/TR (both equal 3/5), the two sides PQ and PR of triangle PQR are divided in the same ratio by line ST.

By Theorem 6.2 (Converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem):
Hypothesis: A line (ST) divides two sides (PQ and PR) of △PQR in the same ratio (3:5).
Conclusion: ST ∥ QR.

Therefore, ST is parallel to QR.
recall_questions.prompt: In △PQR, S is a point on PQ and T is a point on PR. Given PS/SQ = 3/5 and PT/TR = 3/5, determine whether ST ∥ QR. Name the theorem used and state both its hypothesis and conclusion as they apply here.

recall_questions.answer:
In the proof of Theorem 6.2, we have established AE/EC = AE'/E'C.

Adding 1 to both sides:
AE/EC + 1 = AE'/E'C + 1
(AE + EC)/EC = (AE' + E'C)/E'C

Now, AE + EC = AC (the full length of side AC), and AE' + E'C = AC (also the full length). So:
AC/EC = AC/E'C.

Since both sides have the same numerator AC, the denominators must be equal: EC = E'C.

If EC = E'C and both E and E' lie on segment AC starting from C, then E and E' are the same point - they coincide. Since DE' ∥ BC by construction, and DE and DE' are now the same line, DE ∥ BC, contradicting our assumption that DE is not parallel to BC.

carried_over_topics.summary: Three worked examples apply Theorems 6.1 and 6.2 to progressively complex configurations. Example 1 starts from DE ∥ BC and derives AD/AB = AE/AC by taking the reciprocal of the BPT ratio and adding 1 to both sides. Example 2 introduces an auxiliary diagonal AC in a trapezium ABCD and applies Theorem 6.1 separately in △ADC and △CAB to chain two ratio equations into AE/ED = BF/FC. Example 3 uses Theorem 6.2 to establish ST ∥ QR from the given ratio PS/SQ = PT/TR, then combines the resulting angle ST ∥ QR with the given ∠PST = ∠PRQ to show ∠PRQ = ∠PQR, making PQ = PR and triangle PQR isosceles.
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: BPT and its converse are applied to prove three multi-step results: rewriting AD/AB = AE/AC, showing AE/ED = BF/FC in a trapezium with a parallel transversal, and proving triangle PQR is isosceles.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: In Segment 2 you proved Theorem 6.1 (if DE ∥ BC, then AD/DB = AE/EC) and Theorem 6.2 (if AD/DB = AE/EC, then DE ∥ BC). The three worked examples below apply both theorems to multi-step geometric problems. Example 1 is presented with every step and every justification shown. In Example 2, the key insight is set up for you - complete the final line yourself. In Example 3, identify the applicable theorem and write the full proof independently.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Complete (Example 1):
If a line intersects sides AB and AC of △ABC at D and E respectively and is parallel to BC, prove that AD/AB = AE/AC (see Fig. 6.13).

Given: DE ∥ BC.
To prove: AD/AB = AE/AC.

Solution:
DE ∥ BC (Given)
So, AD/DB = AE/EC [Theorem 6.1: a line parallel to BC divides AB and AC in the same ratio]

WHY THIS STEP? Theorem 6.1 applies directly here: D is on AB, E is on AC, and DE ∥ BC.

Taking the reciprocal of both sides: DB/AD = EC/AE.
Adding 1 to both sides: DB/AD + 1 = EC/AE + 1.
(DB + AD)/AD = (EC + AE)/AE.
AB/AD = AC/AE.

WHY THIS STEP? Adding 1 to a fraction a/b gives (a + b)/b. Since DB + AD = AB and EC + AE = AC, the numerators become the full side lengths.

Taking the reciprocal: AD/AB = AE/AC. ☐

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Partially Faded (Example 2):
ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. Points E and F lie on non-parallel sides AD and BC respectively such that EF ∥ AB. Show that AE/ED = BF/FC (see Figs. 6.14-6.15).

Given: AB ∥ DC and EF ∥ AB.
Setup: Join diagonal AC, intersecting EF at G.
Since AB ∥ DC and EF ∥ AB, we have EF ∥ DC (lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other).
In △ADC, EG ∥ DC: so AE/ED = AG/GC by Theorem 6.1 ... (1)
From △CAB, applying Theorem 6.1 to the parallel line GF: CG/GA = CF/FB, i.e., AG/GC = BF/FC ... (2)

Your step: From equations (1) and (2), state the conclusion.

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 - Further Faded (Example 3):
In Fig. 6.16, PS/SQ = PT/TR and ∠PST = ∠PRQ. Prove that △PQR is an isosceles triangle.

Strategy: The condition PS/SQ = PT/TR triggers one of the two BPT theorems. Identify which one and apply it to establish that ST ∥ QR. Then use the angle condition ∠PST = ∠PRQ to show that two angles of △PQR are equal, making two sides equal and the triangle isosceles. Write the complete proof with all justifications.

CHECK: In Example 1, why was it necessary to first take the reciprocal DB/AD = EC/AE before adding 1? What would you get if you added 1 directly to AD/DB = AE/EC, and is the result equivalent?
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Let us take some examples to illustrate the use of the above theorems.
Example 1 : If a line intersects sides AB and AC of a △ABC at D and E respectively and is parallel to BC, prove that AD/AB = AE/AC (see Fig. 6.13).
Solution : DE ∥ BC (Given)
So, AD/DB = AE/EC (Theorem 6.1)
DB/AD = EC/AE
or, DB/AD + 1 = EC/AE + 1
or, AB/AD = AC/AE
So, AD/AB = AE/AC

Example 2 : ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. E and F are points on non-parallel sides AD and BC respectively such that EF is parallel to AB (see Fig. 6.14). Show that AE/ED = BF/FC.
Solution : Let us join AC to intersect EF at G (see Fig. 6.15).
AB ∥ DC and EF ∥ AB (Given)
So, EF ∥ DC (Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other)
Now, in △ADC,
EG ∥ DC (As EF ∥ DC)
So, AE/ED = AG/GC (Theorem 6.1) ... (1)
Similarly, from △CAB,
CG/GA = CF/FB
i.e., AG/GC = BF/FC ... (2)
Therefore, from (1) and (2),
AE/ED = BF/FC

Example 3 : In Fig. 6.16, PS/SQ = PT/TR and ∠PST = ∠PRQ. Prove that PQR is an isosceles triangle.
Solution : It is given that PS/SQ = PT/TR
So, ST ∥ QR (Theorem 6.2)
Therefore, ∠PST = ∠PQR (Corresponding angles) ... (1)
Also, it is given that
∠PST = ∠PRQ ... (2)
So, ∠PRQ = ∠PQR [From (1) and (2)]
Therefore, PQ = PR (Sides opposite the equal angles)
i.e., PQR is an isosceles triangle.
concept_bullets: To convert AD/DB = AE/EC into AD/AB = AE/AC, take the reciprocal first (DB/AD = EC/AE) and then add 1 to both sides - the numerators become AB and AC respectively.

In a trapezium with an auxiliary diagonal, Theorem 6.1 is applied twice in two different triangles sharing the diagonal - for example, in trapezium ABCD with EF ∥ AB, the diagonal AC intersects EF at G, giving AE/ED = AG/GC in △ADC and AG/GC = BF/FC in △CAB.

When a ratio condition PS/SQ = PT/TR is given, Theorem 6.2 immediately yields ST ∥ QR - this parallel conclusion then produces an angle equality that can make two angles of the same triangle equal, forcing the triangle to be isosceles.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: Three worked examples apply Theorems 6.1 and 6.2 to progressively complex configurations. Example 1 starts from DE ∥ BC and derives AD/AB = AE/AC by taking the reciprocal of the BPT ratio and adding 1 to both sides. Example 2 introduces an auxiliary diagonal AC in a trapezium ABCD and applies Theorem 6.1 separately in △ADC and △CAB to chain two ratio equations into AE/ED = BF/FC. Example 3 uses Theorem 6.2 to establish ST ∥ QR from the given ratio PS/SQ = PT/TR, then combines the resulting angle ST ∥ QR with the given ∠PST = ∠PRQ to show ∠PRQ = ∠PQR, making PQ = PR and triangle PQR isosceles.

So, AD/AB = AE/AC
EF ∥ DC (Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other)
ST ∥ QR (Theorem 6.2)
PQ = PR (Sides opposite the equal angles)

Given: DE ∥ BC, so by Theorem 6.1: AD/DB = AE/EC.

Step 1: Take the reciprocal of both sides.
DB/AD = EC/AE.

Step 2: Add 1 to both sides.
DB/AD + 1 = EC/AE + 1
(DB + AD)/AD = (EC + AE)/AE.

carried_over_topics.summary: Exercise 6.2 develops fluency in selecting and applying Theorem 6.1 or Theorem 6.2 across varied geometric configurations. Questions 1-2 require direct substitution into the BPT ratio to find unknown lengths or verify parallelism. Questions 3-4 chain two BPT applications in the same figure through an auxiliary construction. Questions 5-6 extend chaining to three parallel conditions. Questions 7-8 connect BPT to the mid-point theorem by treating the mid-point condition as a ratio of 1:1. Questions 9-10 involve trapezoid diagonals, where an auxiliary diagonal must be drawn to create two triangles before Theorem 6.1 or Theorem 6.2 can be applied. Students practise theorem selection as an explicit step before any algebraic work.
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: Exercise 6.2 is used to practise applying BPT and its converse across ten problems involving unknown lengths, parallel verification, trapezoid diagonals, and the mid-point theorem.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
STRATEGY OVERVIEW: Exercise 6.2 applies Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 6.2 across a range of configurations. Before attempting any question, identify which theorem is relevant.

Use Theorem 6.1 (BPT) when: a line is stated to be parallel to a side of a triangle and you need to derive or use a ratio.
Use Theorem 6.2 (Converse BPT) when: two sides are divided in equal ratios and you need to prove that the dividing line is parallel to the third side.

APPROACH BY QUESTION:

Questions 1-2 (Finding lengths and verifying parallelism):
Q1: DE ∥ BC is given. Write AD/DB = AE/EC by Theorem 6.1, substitute the known values, and solve for the unknown. Keep units consistent throughout.
Q2: For each sub-case, calculate the ratio of the two segments on one side (PE/EQ) and compare it with the ratio on the other side (PF/FR). If equal, EF ∥ QR by Theorem 6.2; if unequal, EF is not parallel to QR.

WORKED EXAMPLE MODEL (Q1, Fig. 6.17(i)):
Given: DE ∥ BC, AD = 1.5 cm, DB = 3 cm, AE = 1 cm. Find EC.
By Theorem 6.1: AD/DB = AE/EC → 1.5/3 = 1/EC → EC = 1 × 3/1.5 = 2 cm.

Questions 3-4 (Chaining two BPT applications):
In Q3, two parallel conditions (LM ∥ CB and LN ∥ CD) are given. Apply Theorem 6.1 separately for each condition in its respective triangle to obtain two ratios, then combine them to reach the target equation AM/AB = AN/AD.
In Q4, apply Theorem 6.1 for the first parallel condition (DE ∥ AC in △ABC) and then the second (DF ∥ AE in △ABE) to build the result BF/FE = BE/EC.

Questions 5-6 (Parallel line chains):
These questions extend the chaining technique to three lines. Establish the first ratio using the given parallel condition, then use that ratio as the input for establishing the next parallel line.

Questions 7-8 (Mid-point theorem connections):
Q7 and Q8 are converses of each other and both connect to the mid-point theorem from Class IX. In Q7, use Theorem 6.1 with the mid-point condition (ratio = 1/1) to show the third side is bisected. In Q8, use Theorem 6.2 with the equal-ratio condition to prove the joining line is parallel to the third side.

Questions 9-10 (Trapezium diagonals):
In Q9, ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. Draw diagonal AC (or BD) to create two triangles. Apply Theorem 6.1 in each triangle, then combine the two ratio equations to arrive at AO/CO = BO/DO. Q10 reverses this: you are given AO/CO = BO/DO and must prove ABCD is a trapezium by showing AB ∥ DC using Theorem 6.2.

ERROR ALERT: When applying Theorem 6.1 to a trapezium, draw an auxiliary diagonal and apply the theorem to each resulting triangle separately. Applying Theorem 6.1 directly to the trapezium without the auxiliary diagonal is not valid - the theorem applies only to triangles.

CHECK: For Q2(iii), PQ = 1.28 cm, PR = 2.56 cm, PE = 0.18 cm, PF = 0.36 cm. First find EQ = PQ − PE and FR = PR − PF. Then compute PE/EQ and PF/FR. Are they equal? State your conclusion about EF ∥ QR.

EXERCISE 6.2
1. In Fig. 6.17, (i) and (ii), DE ∥ BC. Find EC in (i) and AD in (ii).
2. E and F are points on the sides PQ and PR respectively of a △PQR. For each of the following cases, state whether EF ∥ QR :
(i) PE = 3.9 cm, EQ = 3 cm, PF = 3.6 cm and FR = 2.4 cm
(ii) PE = 4 cm, QE = 4.5 cm, PF = 8 cm and RF = 9 cm
(iii) PQ = 1.28 cm, PR = 2.56 cm, PE = 0.18 cm and PF = 0.36 cm
3. In Fig. 6.18, if LM ∥ CB and LN ∥ CD, prove that AM/AB = AN/AD.
4. In Fig. 6.19, DE ∥ AC and DF ∥ AE. Prove that BF/FE = BE/EC.
5. In Fig. 6.20, DE ∥ OQ and DF ∥ OR. Show that EF ∥ QR.
6. In Fig. 6.21, A, B and C are points on OP, OQ and OR respectively such that AB ∥ PQ and AC ∥ PR. Show that BC ∥ QR.
7. Using Theorem 6.1, prove that a line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle parallel to another side bisects the third side. (Recall that you have proved it in Class IX).
8. Using Theorem 6.2, prove that the line joining the mid-points of any two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side. (Recall that you have done it in Class IX).
9. ABCD is a trapezium in which AB ∥ DC and its diagonals intersect each other at the point O. Show that AO/CO = BO/DO.
10. The diagonals of a quadrilateral ABCD intersect each other at the point O such that AO/CO = BO/DO. Show that ABCD is a trapezium.

Given: DE ∥ BC, AD = 1.5 cm, DB = 3 cm, AE = 1 cm. Find EC.

Step 1: Since DE ∥ BC, apply Theorem 6.1 (BPT).
AD/DB = AE/EC.

Step 2: Substitute known values.
1.5/3 = 1/EC.

Step 3: Solve for EC.
EC = (1 × 3)/1.5 = 3/1.5 = 2 cm.

recall_questions.answer:
To test EF ∥ QR, check whether PE/EQ = PF/FR by Theorem 6.2 (Converse BPT).

Step 1: Compute PE/EQ = 3.9/3 = 1.3.

Step 2: Compute PF/FR = 3.6/2.4 = 1.5.

Step 3: Compare: 1.3 ≠ 1.5.

Since PE/EQ ≠ PF/FR, the two sides are not divided in the same ratio. By the contrapositive of Theorem 6.2, EF is NOT parallel to QR.
recall_questions.prompt: For △PQR with E on PQ and F on PR, PE = 3.9 cm, EQ = 3 cm, PF = 3.6 cm, FR = 2.4 cm - determine whether EF ∥ QR. Show your ratio calculations.

recall_questions.answer:
Theorem 6.1 (BPT) applies only to triangles, not directly to quadrilaterals. Therefore, to use BPT in the trapezium ABCD, we must create triangles by drawing an auxiliary diagonal - say AC - to form triangles △DAC and △CAB.

Step 1: In △DAC, OB is parallel to DC (since AB ∥ DC and O lies on both diagonals). Apply Theorem 6.1 to obtain: DO/OB = CO/OA, i.e., AO/CO = BO/DO ... (from this triangle).

Step 2: The same ratio AO/CO = BO/DO is confirmed from △CAB as well, using the parallel lines through O.

The key insight is that without the auxiliary diagonal, there is no triangle in which BPT can be applied. Drawing AC creates the required triangular context.

carried_over_topics.summary: Similarity notation △ABC ∼ △DEF declares that A corresponds to D, B to E, and C to F; the vertex order is mandatory and incorrect ordering produces wrong ratio equations. Activity 4 demonstrates that two triangles with BC = 3 cm and EF = 5 cm and the same three angle measures yield AB/DE = CA/FD = BC/EF = 0.6, showing that equal angles force proportional sides. Theorem 6.3 (AAA criterion) formalises this observation, with a proof sketch using an auxiliary triangle DPQ congruent to △ABC by SAS and applying BPT to establish the side ratios. The AA corollary follows immediately from the angle sum property: confirming two angle equalities is sufficient, since the third is determined.
carried_over_topics.topic_name: Similarity Notation and the AAA Criterion
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: The AAA similarity criterion (Theorem 6.3) states that if corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, then their corresponding sides are proportional and the triangles are similar.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: All results so far - the definition of similar polygons, Theorem 6.1, and Theorem 6.2 - have been established in Segment 1 and Segment 2. In this topic you extend the investigation to specific criteria that tell you when two triangles are similar without checking all six equalities.

CORE - Similarity Notation:
When two triangles △ABC and △DEF satisfy both similarity conditions:
(i)  ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F, and
(ii) AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD,
we write △ABC ∼ △DEF (read: ‘triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF’).

The symbol ‘∼’ stands for ‘is similar to’. This is distinct from ‘≅’, which stands for ‘is congruent to’. Similarity preserves shape; congruence preserves both shape and size.

The order of vertices in the notation is critical: writing △ABC ∼ △DEF declares that A corresponds to D, B to E, and C to F. Therefore △ABC ∼ △EDF is incorrect unless E corresponds to A, D to B, and F to C. However, △BAC ∼ △EDF is correct if B corresponds to E, A to D, and C to F. Always verify the correspondence before writing the symbolic form.

WHY NOTATION MATTERS: The corresponding-sides ratios and corresponding-angle equalities depend entirely on the declared vertex correspondence. An incorrectly ordered similarity statement leads to wrong ratio equations.

CAN WE CHECK FEWER THAN SIX CONDITIONS?
In Class IX, congruency criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) required only three matching parts. There are analogous similarity criteria for triangles. Activity 4 establishes the first.

Activity 4: Draw segments BC = 3 cm and EF = 5 cm. Construct angles PBC = QCB = 60° and 40° at B and C, and angles REF = SFE = 60° and 40° at E and F respectively. Let rays BP and CQ meet at A, and rays ER and FS meet at D (see Figs. 6.22-6.23). In △ABC and △DEF: ∠B = ∠E = 60° and ∠C = ∠F = 40°, so ∠A = ∠D = 80°. The triangles are equiangular. Measure AB, DE, CA, FD: you will find AB/DE = CA/FD = BC/EF = 3/5 = 0.6. Proportional sides follow automatically from the equal angles.

Repeating Activity 4 for different angle combinations always gives the same result. This leads to Theorem 6.3.

Theorem 6.3 (AAA Similarity Criterion): If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio and hence the two triangles are similar.

Proof sketch (see Fig. 6.24): Given △ABC and △DEF with ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F. Cut DP = AB and DQ = AC and join PQ.
Since DP = AB, ∠D = ∠A, and DQ = AC: △ABC ≅ △DPQ (SAS congruency). Therefore ∠B = ∠P. Since ∠P = ∠E, we get PQ ∥ EF.
WHY? Equal corresponding angles with transversal DE imply PQ ∥ EF.
Applying Theorem 6.1 to △DEF: DP/PE = DQ/QF, giving AB/DE = AC/DF. Similarly AB/DE = BC/EF. Hence △ABC ∼ △DEF.

AA COROLLARY: If two pairs of corresponding angles are equal, the third pair is automatically equal by the angle sum property (180° minus the two known angles). Therefore, AA (just two angle equalities) is sufficient for similarity. This is the AA similarity criterion.

An important contrast: recall from Segment 1 that at a marble showroom in Jaipur, two rhombus-shaped tiles with equal angles (60° each) turned out to be non-similar because their sides were not proportional. For general polygons, equal angles alone do not imply similarity. For triangles, Theorem 6.3 shows this restriction disappears - equal angles automatically force proportional sides, a property unique to triangles.

ERROR ALERT: When applying the AAA criterion, you need all three pairs of corresponding angles to be equal. The AA corollary allows you to stop after confirming two pairs and invoking the angle sum property for the third. Do not use the AAA criterion for quadrilaterals or other polygons - it does not generalise beyond triangles.

CHECK: In Activity 4, BC = 3 cm and EF = 5 cm. If you measure AB = 4.2 cm, what should DE equal? Set up the ratio equation AB/DE = BC/EF = 3/5, substitute AB = 4.2, and solve for DE.
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
6.4 Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
In the previous section, we stated that two triangles are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion). That is, in △ABC and △DEF, if
(i) ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F and
(ii) AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD, then the two triangles are similar (see Fig. 6.22).
Here, you can see that A corresponds to D, B corresponds to E and C corresponds to F. Symbolically, we write the similarity of these two triangles as '△ABC ~ △DEF' and read it as 'triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF'. The symbol '~' stands for 'is similar to'. Recall that you have used the symbol '≅' for 'is congruent to' in Class IX.
It must be noted that as done in the case of congruency of two triangles, the similarity of two triangles should also be expressed symbolically, using correct correspondence of their vertices. For example, for the triangles ABC and DEF of Fig. 6.22, we cannot write △ABC ~ △EDF or △ABC ~ △FED. However, we can write △BAC ~ △EDF.
Now a natural question arises : For checking the similarity of two triangles, say ABC and DEF, should we always look for all the equality relations of their corresponding angles (∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F) and all the equality relations of the ratios of their corresponding sides (AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD)? Let us examine. You may recall that in Class IX, you have obtained some criteria for congruency of two triangles involving only three pairs of corresponding parts (or elements) of the two triangles. Here also, let us make an attempt to arrive at certain criteria for similarity of two triangles involving relationship between less number of pairs of corresponding parts of the two triangles, instead of all the six pairs of corresponding parts. For this, let us perform the following activity:
Activity 4 : Draw two line segments BC and EF of two different lengths, say 3 cm and 5 cm respectively. Then, at the points B and C respectively, construct angles PBC and QCB of some measures, say, 60° and 40°. Also, at the points E and F, construct angles REF and SFE of 60° and 40° respectively (see Fig. 6.23).
Let rays BP and CQ intersect each other at A and rays ER and FS intersect each other at D. In the two triangles ABC and DEF, you can see that ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F and ∠A = ∠D. That is, corresponding angles of these two triangles are equal. Note that BC/EF = 3/5 = 0.6. On measuring AB, DE, CA and FD, you will find that AB/DE and CA/FD are also equal to 0.6 (or nearly equal to 0.6, if there is some error in the measurement). Thus, AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD. You can repeat this activity by constructing several pairs of triangles having their corresponding angles equal. Every time, you will find that their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion). This activity leads us to the following criterion for similarity of two triangles.
Theorem 6.3 : If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion) and hence the two triangles are similar.
This criterion is referred to as the AAA (Angle-Angle-Angle) criterion of similarity of two triangles.
This theorem can be proved by taking two triangles ABC and DEF such that ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F (see Fig. 6.24). Cut DP = AB and DQ = AC and join PQ.
So, △ABC ≅ △DPQ (Why?)
This gives ∠B = ∠P = ∠E and PQ ∥ EF (How?)
Therefore, DP/PE = DQ/QF (Why?)
i.e., AB/DE = AC/DF (Why?)
Similarly, AB/DE = BC/EF and so AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF.
Remark : If two angles of a triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then by the angle sum property of a triangle their third angles will also be equal. Therefore, AAA similarity criterion can also be stated as follows:
If two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are similar.
This may be referred to as the AA similarity criterion for two triangles.
concept_bullets: The AAA criterion for triangles - three equal angle pairs guarantee similar triangles - does not extend to general polygons: two quadrilaterals can have all four corresponding angles equal (as with a square and a rectangle with all right angles) and still not be similar.
The AA corollary is sufficient in practice: once ∠B = ∠E = 60° and ∠C = ∠F = 40° are verified, the third angles are both 180° − 60° − 40° = 80°, confirming AAA without direct measurement.
In Activity 4 with BC = 3 cm and EF = 5 cm, the scale factor is BC/EF = 3/5 = 0.6, so AB/DE and CA/FD must also equal 0.6 - verifiable by measurement.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: Similarity notation △ABC ∼ △DEF declares that A corresponds to D, B to E, and C to F; the vertex order is mandatory and incorrect ordering produces wrong ratio equations. Activity 4 demonstrates that two triangles with BC = 3 cm and EF = 5 cm and the same three angle measures yield AB/DE = CA/FD = BC/EF = 0.6, showing that equal angles force proportional sides. Theorem 6.3 (AAA criterion) formalises this observation, with a proof sketch using an auxiliary triangle DPQ congruent to △ABC by SAS and applying BPT to establish the side ratios. The AA corollary follows immediately from the angle sum property: confirming two angle equalities is sufficient, since the third is determined.
important_points: Theorem 6.3 : If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion) and hence the two triangles are similar.
If two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are similar.
AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD.

Angle equalities: ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F.

Side-ratio equalities: AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD = k, where k is the scale factor.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: By the AAA similarity criterion (Theorem 6.3), △ABC ∼ △DEF with BC = 3 cm, EF = 5 cm, AB = 4.2 cm.

Step 1: From the similarity, corresponding sides are proportional:
AB/DE = BC/EF.

Step 2: Substitute known values:
4.2/DE = 3/5.

Step 3: Cross-multiply:
4.2 × 5 = 3 × DE
21 = 3 × DE.

Step 4: Solve for DE:
DE = 21/3 = 7 cm.

Therefore, DE = 7 cm.

recall_questions.answer:
AA Similarity Criterion (Corollary to Theorem 6.3): If two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are similar.

Two angle equalities are sufficient because the three interior angles of any triangle always sum to 180°. If two pairs of angles are equal, the third pair is automatically determined:
If ∠A = ∠D and ∠B = ∠E, then ∠C = 180° − ∠A − ∠B = 180° − ∠D − ∠E = ∠F.

Therefore, knowing two angle equalities gives all three - and all three angle equalities together satisfy the AAA criterion (Theorem 6.3), which guarantees similarity.

RECALL: Theorem 6.3 established that equal corresponding angles in two triangles guarantee proportional sides. Activity 5 now asks the converse: if two triangles have all three pairs of sides proportional, must their angles be equal?

Activity 5: Draw △ABC with AB = 3 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 8 cm, and △DEF with DE = 4.5 cm, EF = 9 cm, FD = 12 cm (see Fig. 6.25). Verify that AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD = 2/3. Now measure all six angles. You will find ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F. Repeating this for other proportional triples always gives equal angles. This leads to Theorem 6.4.

THEOREM STATEMENT:
Theorem 6.4 (SSS Similarity Criterion): If in two triangles, sides of one triangle are proportional to the sides of the other triangle, then their corresponding angles are equal and hence the two triangles are similar.

GIVEN:
△ABC and △DEF such that AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD, with this common ratio less than 1 (so △ABC is the smaller triangle) (see Fig. 6.26).

TO PROVE:
∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F, and △ABC ∼ △DEF.

CONSTRUCTION:
On DE, cut DP = AB. On DF, cut DQ = AC. Join PQ.

PROOF STEPS:

(i) Establish DP/PE = DQ/QF:
    DP/DE = AB/DE and DQ/DF = AC/DF.
    Since AB/DE = CA/FD (given), DP/DE = DQ/DF.
    Therefore DP/PE = DQ/QF.
    WHY? If DP/DE = DQ/DF, then (DE − DP)/DP = (DF − DQ)/DQ, i.e., PE/DP = QF/DQ, which rearranges to DP/PE = DQ/QF.
    By Theorem 6.2 (Converse BPT), PQ ∥ EF. ... (*)

(ii) From (*), ∠P = ∠E and ∠Q = ∠F (corresponding angles, PQ ∥ EF).
    Therefore △DPQ ∼ △DEF (by AA), giving DP/DE = DQ/DF = PQ/EF.

(iii) From (ii): PQ/EF = DP/DE = AB/DE = BC/EF (by the given proportionality).
    Therefore PQ = BC.
    WHY? If PQ/EF = BC/EF, the denominators cancel, giving PQ = BC directly.

(iv) Compare △ABC and △DPQ:
    AB = DP (construction), BC = PQ (step iii), CA = QD (construction).
    Therefore △ABC ≅ △DPQ by SSS congruency from Class IX.
    WHY? All three pairs of sides are equal, which is exactly the SSS congruency condition.

(v) From the congruency: ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠P = ∠E, ∠C = ∠Q = ∠F.

CONCLUSION:
The corresponding angles of △ABC and △DEF are all equal, so △ABC ∼ △DEF. □

Remark: Compare SSS similarity with SSS congruency. In SSS congruency (Class IX), three equal pairs of sides guarantee identical triangles. In SSS similarity, three proportional pairs of sides guarantee similar shape but not necessarily equal size.

ERROR ALERT: Step (i) requires careful algebra: from AB/DE = CA/FD, you must derive DP/PE = DQ/QF (not simply assert it). Write out each algebraic step. Then invoke Theorem 6.2 explicitly with its hypothesis stated.

CHECK: Two triangles have sides 4 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm and 8 cm, 12 cm, 18 cm respectively. Verify that the ratios of all three corresponding pairs of sides are equal, and state which theorem guarantees the triangles are similar.

You have seen above that if the three angles of one triangle are respectively equal to the three angles of another triangle, then their corresponding sides are proportional (i.e., in the same ratio). What about the converse of this statement? Is the converse true? In other words, if the sides of a triangle are respectively proportional to the sides of another triangle, is it true that their corresponding angles are equal? Let us examine it through an activity :
Activity 5 : Draw two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB = 3 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 8 cm, DE = 4.5 cm, EF = 9 cm and FD = 12 cm (see Fig. 6.25).
So, you have : AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD = 2/3.
Now measure ∠A, ∠B, ∠C, ∠D, ∠E and ∠F. You will observe that ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F, i.e., the corresponding angles of the two triangles are equal.
You can repeat this activity by drawing several such triangles (having their sides in the same ratio). Everytime you shall see that their corresponding angles are equal. It is due to the following criterion of similarity of two triangles:
Theorem 6.4 : If in two triangles, sides of one triangle are proportional to (i.e., in the same ratio of) the sides of the other triangle, then their corresponding angles are equal and hence the two triangles are similar.
This criterion is referred to as the SSS (Side-Side-Side) similarity criterion for two triangles.
This theorem can be proved by taking two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD (< 1) (see Fig. 6.26):
Cut DP = AB and DQ = AC and join PQ.
It can be seen that DP/PE = DQ/QF and PQ ∥ EF (How?)
So, ∠P = ∠E and ∠Q = ∠F.
Therefore, DP/DE = DQ/DF = PQ/EF
So, DP/DE = DQ/DF = BC/EF (Why?)
So, BC = PQ (Why?)
Thus, △ABC ≅ △DPQ (Why?)
So, ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F (How?)
Remark : You may recall that either of the two conditions namely, (i) corresponding angles are equal and (ii) corresponding sides are in the same ratio is not sufficient for two polygons to be similar. However, on the basis of Theorems 6.3 and 6.4, you can now say that in case of similarity of the two triangles, it is not necessary to check both the conditions as one condition implies the other.
concept_bullets: The SSS similarity criterion requires all three side-ratio pairs to be equal - for example, triangles with sides 4, 6, 9 and 8, 12, 18 cm have ratios 4/8 = 6/12 = 9/18 = 1/2, confirming SSS similarity with scale factor 1/2.

To prove SSS similarity, the auxiliary cut DP = AB and DQ = AC inside △DEF creates a smaller triangle DPQ that is congruent to △ABC by SSS congruency - then angles transfer from DPQ to DEF through the parallel line PQ ∥ EF.
SSS similarity differs from SSS congruency: congruency requires three equal side pairs (scale factor = 1), while similarity only requires three proportional side pairs (any scale factor).

Corresponding angles then give ∠P = ∠E, and the ratio chain forces PQ = BC, after which SSS congruency △ABC ≅ △DPQ completes the proof by delivering the required angle equalities.

Theorem 6.4 (SSS Similarity Criterion): If in two triangles, the sides of one triangle are proportional to the sides of the other triangle, then their corresponding angles are equal and the two triangles are similar.

Difference from SSS congruency: In SSS congruency (Class IX), the three corresponding sides must be equal in length (scale factor = 1). In SSS similarity, the three corresponding sides only need to be proportional - in the same ratio - but do not need to be equal. Congruency is the special case of similarity when the scale factor is exactly 1.

recall_questions.answer:
Let △ABC have sides AB = 4 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 9 cm. Let △DEF have sides DE = 8 cm, EF = 12 cm, FD = 18 cm.

Step 1: Compute the ratios of corresponding sides (matching shortest to shortest, middle to middle, longest to longest).
AB/DE = 4/8 = 1/2.
BC/EF = 6/12 = 1/2.
CA/FD = 9/18 = 1/2.

Step 2: All three ratios are equal (each = 1/2). So the sides of △ABC are proportional to the sides of △DEF.

Step 3: By Theorem 6.4 (SSS Similarity Criterion), the corresponding angles are equal and △ABC ∼ △DEF with scale factor 1/2.
recall_questions.prompt: Two triangles have sides 4 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm and 8 cm, 12 cm, 18 cm respectively. Verify that the SSS similarity criterion applies and write the similarity statement with correct vertex labelling.

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1 - Deducing PQ = BC:
From PQ ∥ EF, triangles △DPQ ∼ △DEF by AA (since ∠P = ∠E and ∠Q = ∠F from corresponding angles). Therefore DP/DE = DQ/DF = PQ/EF.
Now DP/DE = AB/DE (by construction, DP = AB). From the given proportionality AB/DE = BC/EF. Therefore PQ/EF = BC/EF, which gives PQ = BC.

Step 2 - Applying SSS congruency:
Compare △ABC and △DPQ:
- AB = DP (by construction),
- BC = PQ (proved above),
- CA = QD (by construction, DQ = AC).
All three pairs of sides are equal. By the SSS congruency criterion from Class IX, △ABC ≅ △DPQ. Therefore ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠P = ∠E, ∠C = ∠Q = ∠F, giving all three angle equalities. Hence △ABC ∼ △DEF. □

carried_over_topics.summary: The SAS similarity criterion mirrors the SAS congruency condition but replaces equal sides with proportional sides; the included angle condition is identical. Activity 6 demonstrates this with △ABC (AB = 2, ∠A = 50°, AC = 4) and △DEF (DE = 3, ∠D = 50°, DF = 6), where AB/DE = AC/DF = 2/3 and all three angle pairs prove equal upon measurement. The proof follows the same auxiliary-cut technique as Theorem 6.4: cut DP = AB and DQ = AC inside △DEF, establish △ABC ≅ △DPQ by SAS congruency, derive PQ ∥ EF through Theorem 6.2, and use corresponding angles to transfer ∠E and ∠F to the original triangles. carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: SSS similarity (Theorem 6.4) requires all three pairs of sides to be proportional. From Class IX you also know the SAS congruency criterion: two sides and the included angle matching guarantees congruent triangles. Activity 6 explores the analogous question for similarity: is one equal included angle combined with proportional sides on either side sufficient?

Activity 6: Draw △ABC with AB = 2 cm, ∠A = 50°, AC = 4 cm, and △DEF with DE = 3 cm, ∠D = 50°, DF = 6 cm (see Fig. 6.27). Verify AB/DE = AC/DF = 2/3 and ∠A = ∠D = 50° (each is the included angle between the two proportional sides). Measure ∠B, ∠C, ∠E, ∠F. You will find ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F, so all three angle pairs are equal and △ABC ∼ △DEF by AAA (Theorem 6.3).

Repeating Activity 6 for different angles and side ratios always yields similar triangles. This leads to Theorem 6.5.

THEOREM STATEMENT:
Theorem 6.5 (SAS Similarity Criterion): If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of the other triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two triangles are similar.

GIVEN:
△ABC and △DEF such that AB/DE = AC/DF (ratio < 1) and ∠A = ∠D, where ∠A is the included angle between AB and AC, and ∠D is the included angle between DE and DF (see Fig. 6.28).

TO PROVE:
△ABC ∼ △DEF.

CONSTRUCTION:
On DE, cut DP = AB. On DF, cut DQ = AC. Join PQ.

PROOF STEPS:

(i) Establish △ABC ≅ △DPQ:
    DP = AB (construction), ∠D = ∠A (given), DQ = AC (construction).
    WHY? This is exactly the SAS congruency criterion from Class IX: two sides and the included angle match.
    Therefore △ABC ≅ △DPQ, giving ∠B = ∠P.

(ii) Establish PQ ∥ EF:
    DP/DE = AB/DE and DQ/DF = AC/DF. Since AB/DE = AC/DF (given), DP/DE = DQ/DF, so DP/PE = DQ/QF.
    WHY? The algebra is identical to step (i) of Theorem 6.4’s proof.
    By Theorem 6.2, PQ ∥ EF.

(iii) From PQ ∥ EF, corresponding angles give ∠P = ∠E and ∠Q = ∠F.
    Combining with ∠B = ∠P (step i): ∠B = ∠E.
    Since ∠A = ∠D (given) and ∠B = ∠E, the angle sum property gives ∠C = ∠F.
    Therefore △ABC ∼ △DEF (all three angle pairs equal - AAA). □

CONCLUSION:
If AB/DE = AC/DF and ∠A = ∠D (included), then △ABC ∼ △DEF. □

ERROR ALERT: SAS similarity requires the equal angle to be the included angle - the angle formed between the two sides whose ratios are given. This matches the SAS congruency requirement. If the equal angle is not between the two proportional sides, the SAS criterion does not apply. Always confirm which angle is included before using Theorem 6.5.

CHECK: In △PQR and △STU, PQ/ST = QR/TU = 2/5 and ∠Q = ∠T. Is ∠Q the included angle between the sides PQ and QR in △PQR? Is ∠T the included angle between ST and TU in △STU? If so, which theorem applies? Write the full similarity statement with correct vertex correspondence.
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Let us now recall the various criteria for congruency of two triangles learnt in Class IX. You may observe that SSS similarity criterion can be compared with the SSS congruency criterion. This suggests us to look for a similarity criterion comparable to SAS congruency criterion of triangles. For this, let us perform an activity.
Activity 6 : Draw two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB = 2 cm, ∠A = 50°, AC = 4 cm, DE = 3 cm, ∠D = 50° and DF = 6 cm (see Fig.6.27).
Here, you may observe that AB/DE = AC/DF = 2/3 and ∠A (included between the sides AB and AC) = ∠D (included between the sides DE and DF). That is, one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and sides including these angles are in the same ratio (i.e., proportion). Now let us measure ∠B, ∠C, ∠E and ∠F.
You will find that ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F. That is, ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F. So, by AAA similarity criterion, △ABC ~ △DEF. You may repeat this activity by drawing several pairs of such triangles with one angle of a triangle equal to one angle of another triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional. Everytime, you will find that the triangles are similar. It is due to the following criterion of similarity of triangles:
Theorem 6.5 : If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of the other triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two triangles are similar.
This criterion is referred to as the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) similarity criterion for two triangles.
As before, this theorem can be proved by taking two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB/DE = AC/DF (< 1) and ∠A = ∠D (see Fig. 6.28). Cut DP = AB, DQ = AC and join PQ.
Now, PQ ∥ EF and △ABC ≅ △DPQ (How?)
So, ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠P and ∠C = ∠Q
Therefore, △ABC ~ △DEF (Why?)
concept_bullets: SAS similarity requires the equal angle to be the included angle - for example, in △ABC and △DEF with AB/DE = AC/DF = 2/3 and ∠A = ∠D = 50°, the angle is between sides AB and AC (and between DE and DF), so SAS applies and △ABC ∼ △DEF.

If the equal angle is not the included angle, SAS similarity cannot be claimed - for example, if ∠A = ∠D but ∠A is opposite to one of the proportional sides rather than between them, a different criterion must be sought.

SAS similarity differs from SAS congruency only in the side condition: congruency needs AB = DE and AC = DF, while similarity needs AB/DE = AC/DF as a common ratio, with ∠A = ∠D included in both cases.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: The SAS similarity criterion mirrors the SAS congruency condition but replaces equal sides with proportional sides; the included angle condition is identical. Activity 6 demonstrates this with △ABC (AB = 2, ∠A = 50°, AC = 4) and △DEF (DE = 3, ∠D = 50°, DF = 6), where AB/DE = AC/DF = 2/3 and all three angle pairs prove equal upon measurement. The proof follows the same auxiliary-cut technique as Theorem 6.4: cut DP = AB and DQ = AC inside △DEF, establish △ABC ≅ △DPQ by SAS congruency, derive PQ ∥ EF through Theorem 6.2, and use corresponding angles to transfer ∠E and ∠F to the original triangles. The critical requirement is that the equal angle must be the included angle between the two proportional sides.
important_points: Theorem 6.5 : If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of the other triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two triangles are similar.
AB/DE = AC/DF = 2/3 and ∠A (included between the sides AB and AC) = ∠D (included between the sides DE and DF).
Now, PQ ∥ EF and △ABC ≅ △DPQ (How?)

recall_questions.answer:
Theorem 6.5 (SAS Similarity Criterion): If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two triangles are similar.

Critical requirement: The equal angle must be the INCLUDED angle - the angle formed between the two sides whose ratios are given. In SSS similarity, only side proportionality is required. In SAS similarity, proportional sides alone are not sufficient; the equal angle must specifically lie between those two proportional sides in each triangle. If the equal angle is not the included angle, SAS similarity does not apply.

Check the SAS condition:
- The proportional sides are AB and PQ (from side AB), and AC and PR (from side AC). The ratio AB/PQ = AC/PR = 2/5.
- The angle ∠A is included between sides AB and AC in △ABC.
- The angle ∠P is included between sides PQ and PR in △PQR.
- ∠A = ∠P = 65°. ✓

Both conditions hold: AB/PQ = AC/PR and the equal angle (65°) is the included angle between the two proportional sides in both triangles.

By Theorem 6.5 (SAS Similarity Criterion), △ABC ∼ △PQR.

Vertex correspondence: A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R.
recall_questions.prompt: In △ABC and △PQR, AB/PQ = AC/PR = 2/5 and ∠A = ∠P = 65°. Determine whether the SAS similarity criterion applies and, if so, write the similarity statement.

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1 - Proving △ABC ≅ △DPQ:
DP = AB (by construction), ∠D = ∠A (given, this is the included angle), DQ = AC (by construction). These three quantities - two sides and the included angle - match exactly the SAS congruency criterion from Class IX. Therefore △ABC ≅ △DPQ.

Step 2 - Role of Theorem 6.2:
From the given condition AB/DE = AC/DF and the construction DP = AB, DQ = AC, we get DP/DE = DQ/DF, which gives DP/PE = DQ/QF. By Theorem 6.2 (Converse BPT), since point P on DE and point Q on DF satisfy this ratio equality, PQ ∥ EF.

From PQ ∥ EF: ∠P = ∠E (corresponding angles). From the congruency, ∠B = ∠P. Therefore ∠B = ∠E. Combined with ∠A = ∠D, the angle sum gives ∠C = ∠F. All three angle pairs are equal, so △ABC ∼ △DEF by AAA. □

RECALL: You now have three similarity criteria at your disposal: AAA/AA (Theorem 6.3), SSS (Theorem 6.4), and SAS (Theorem 6.5). The three worked examples below apply all three. WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Complete (Example 4):
In Fig. 6.29, if PQ ∥ RS, prove that △POQ ∼ △SOR.

Solution:
∠P = ∠S [Alternate interior angles: PQ ∥ RS with transversal PS]
∠Q = ∠R [Alternate interior angles: PQ ∥ RS with transversal QR]
∠POQ = ∠SOR [Vertically opposite angles at the intersection point O]
Therefore, △POQ ∼ △SOR [AAA similarity criterion]. ☐

We now take some examples to illustrate the use of these criteria.
Example 4 : In Fig. 6.29, if PQ ∥ RS, prove that △POQ ~ △SOR.

So, ∠P = ∠S (Alternate angles)
and ∠Q = ∠R

Therefore, ∠C = ∠P (Corresponding angles of similar triangles)

= 180° − 80° − 60° = 40°

CA/PR = 3√3/6√3 = 1/2.

Step 2: All three ratios equal 1/2. By Theorem 6.4 (SSS Similarity Criterion), △ABC ∼ △RQP.

Step 3: From the vertex correspondence (A↔R, B↔Q, C↔P): ∠C = ∠P.

Step 4: Find ∠C using the angle sum in △ABC:
∠C = 180° − ∠A − ∠B = 180° − 80° − 60° = 40°.

Therefore, ∠P = ∠C = 40°.

carried_over_topics.summary: Indirect measurement using similar triangles is illustrated through the lamp-post shadow problem. The girl CD = 0.9 m and the lamp AB = 3.6 m are both perpendicular to the ground, giving ∠B = ∠D = 90°. The shadow tip E is a common vertex, giving ∠E = ∠E. Two angle equalities make △ABE ∼ △CDE by AA similarity. The proportion BE/DE = AB/CD with BE = BD + DE = 4.8 + x and CD = 0.9 gives (4.8 + x)/x = 4, which solves to x = 1.6 m. The same technique applies to any indirect-measurement problem where two vertical objects are illuminated by the same light source.
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: AA similarity is used to solve the lamp-post shadow problem, where a girl walking away from a lamp forms two similar triangles whose proportional sides yield the shadow length of 1.6 m.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
THE PROBLEM (in words):
A girl of height 90 cm is walking away from the base of a lamp-post at a speed of 1.2 m/s. The lamp is 3.6 m above the ground. Find the length of her shadow after 4 seconds.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?:
A vertical lamp-post AB casts light that creates a shadow DE of a girl CD walking away from the lamp along level ground. After 4 seconds of walking at 1.2 m/s, the shadow’s length is required.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
• CD = 0.9 m (girl’s height: 90 cm = 0.9 m)
• AB = 3.6 m (height of the lamp)
• Speed = 1.2 m/s; time = 4 s; so BD = 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 m (distance walked)
• DE = x metres (shadow length - unknown)

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?:
The value of x (the length DE of the shadow) after 4 seconds.

TRANSLATE TO MATHS:
In △ABE and △CDE (see Fig. 6.32):
∠B = ∠D = 90° (both the lamp-post and the girl are perpendicular to the ground)
∠E = ∠E (same angle at the tip of the shadow)
Therefore △ABE ∼ △CDE [AA similarity criterion].

SOLVE:
Corresponding sides: BE/DE = AB/CD
(BD + DE)/DE = AB/CD [since BE = BD + DE]
(4.8 + x)/x = 3.6/0.9 = 4
4.8 + x = 4x
3x = 4.8
x = 1.6 m

CHECK AGAINST THE SITUATION:
The shadow is 1.6 m long. Since the lamp (3.6 m) is four times the girl’s height (0.9 m), a 1.6 m shadow for a 4.8 m walk is physically reasonable. This indirect-measurement technique - using similar triangles formed by a vertical object and its shadow - is equally applicable to finding the height of a flagpole, a tree, or a building, provided the same light source (the sun) casts both shadows simultaneously.

WHY THE AA CRITERION?
Two angle equalities are sufficient: both right angles (∠B = ∠D = 90°) are directly observable because both objects stand vertically, and the common angle at E follows from the shadow tip being a single point. No side measurements are needed to establish similarity.

ERROR ALERT: The distance BE from the lamp-post base to the shadow tip equals BD + DE = 4.8 + x, not just 4.8. Writing BE = 4.8 m is incorrect because the shadow DE extends beyond D. Always express BE as the sum of the two sub-segments before setting up the ratio.

CHECK: If the girl had been walking at 1.8 m/s instead of 1.2 m/s, the distance BD after 4 seconds would be 1.8 × 4 = 7.2 m. With the lamp still at 3.6 m and the girl still at 0.9 m, set up the proportion and find the new shadow length x.
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Example 7 : A girl of height 90 cm is walking away from the base of a lamp-post at a speed of 1.2 m/s. If the lamp is 3.6 m above the ground, find the length of her shadow after 4 seconds.
Solution : Let AB denote the lamp-post and CD the girl after walking for 4 seconds away from the lamp-post (see Fig. 6.32). From the figure, you can see that DE is the shadow of the girl. Let DE be x metres.
Now, BD = 1.2 m × 4 = 4.8 m.
Note that in △ABE and △CDE,
∠B = ∠D (Each is of 90° because lamp-post as well as the girl are standing vertical to the ground)
and ∠E = ∠E (Same angle)
So, △ABE ~ △CDE (AA similarity criterion)
Therefore, BE/DE = AB/CD
(4.8 + x)/x = 3.6/0.9 (90 cm = 90/100 m = 0.9 m)
i.e., 4.8 + x = 4x
i.e., 3x = 4.8
i.e., x = 1.6
So, the shadow of the girl after walking for 4 seconds is 1.6 m long.
concept_bullets: When two vertical objects stand on level ground and are illuminated by the same light source, they form two similar triangles by AA - for example, a 3.6 m lamp and a 0.9 m girl both make 90° with the ground (∠B = ∠D = 90°) and share the angle at the shadow tip E.
The distance BE from the lamp base to the shadow tip equals BD + DE, not just BD - for example, with BD = 4.8 m and shadow DE = x, BE = 4.8 + x must be used in the proportion (4.8 + x)/x = 3.6/0.9.

This indirect measurement technique gives height h of any vertical object using the proportion (known distance + shadow)/shadow = (known height)/(object height), as in the pole example: 6/4 = h/28 giving h = 42 m.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: Indirect measurement using similar triangles is illustrated through the lamp-post shadow problem. The girl CD = 0.9 m and the lamp AB = 3.6 m are both perpendicular to the ground, giving ∠B = ∠D = 90°. The shadow tip E is a common vertex, giving ∠E = ∠E. Two angle equalities make △ABE ∼ △CDE by AA similarity. The proportion BE/DE = AB/CD with BE = BD + DE = 4.8 + x and CD = 0.9 gives (4.8 + x)/x = 4, which solves to x = 1.6 m. The same technique applies to any indirect-measurement problem where two vertical objects are illuminated by the same light source.
important_points: ∠B = ∠D (Each is of 90° because lamp-post as well as the girl are standing vertical to the ground)
△ABE ~ △CDE (AA similarity criterion)
BE/DE = AB/CD
the shadow of the girl after walking for 4 seconds is 1.6 m long.

recall_questions.answer:
After 4 seconds, BD = 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 m (distance from lamp-post base to girl's position).

The two triangles are △ABE (lamp-post, ground, and shadow tip) and △CDE (girl, ground, and shadow tip), where E is the tip of the shadow.

Two angle equalities for AA:
(i) ∠B = ∠D = 90° - both the lamp-post AB and the girl CD stand vertically on level ground, so each forms a right angle with the ground.
(ii) ∠E = ∠E - the same angle at the shadow tip E is shared by both triangles.

By the AA similarity criterion, △ABE ∼ △CDE.
recall_questions.prompt: In the lamp-post shadow problem, a girl of height 0.9 m walks at 1.2 m/s away from a 3.6 m lamp-post. Identify the two triangles formed after 4 seconds and state the two angle equalities that justify the AA similarity criterion.

recall_questions.answer:
From △ABE ∼ △CDE, corresponding sides are proportional:
BE/DE = AB/CD.

Step 1: Express BE in terms of known quantities.
BE = BD + DE = 4.8 + x.

Step 2: Set up the proportion.
(4.8 + x)/x = 3.6/0.9 = 4.

Step 3: Solve.
4.8 + x = 4x
4.8 = 4x − x = 3x
x = 4.8/3 = 1.6 m.

Therefore, the length of the shadow after 4 seconds is 1.6 m.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the AA similarity of △ABE and △CDE (AB = 3.6 m, CD = 0.9 m, BD = 4.8 m, shadow DE = x m), set up the proportion and solve for x. Show all steps.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Measuring rod height = 1 m, its shadow = 1.2 m. Flagpole shadow = 7.8 m. Find flagpole height h.

Step 1: Both the rod and the flagpole are vertical (right angle with ground). Both shadows are cast by the sun at the same angle of elevation at the same time. By AA similarity, the rod-shadow triangle is similar to the flagpole-shadow triangle.

Step 2: Set up the proportion.
rod height / rod shadow = flagpole height / flagpole shadow
1/1.2 = h/7.8.

Step 3: Cross-multiply.
1.2 × h = 1 × 7.8
h = 7.8/1.2 = 6.5 m.

Therefore, the height of the flagpole is 6.5 m.
