carried_over_topics.summary: Example 8 demonstrates multi-step similarity reasoning using medians. Given △ABC ∼ △PQR with medians CM and RN, the proof of Part (i) derives AM/PN = CA/RP from the parent similarity ratio AB/PQ = CA/RP and the median condition AB = 2AM, PQ = 2PN, then combines it with ∠MAC = ∠NPR (given by the parent similarity) to conclude △AMC ∼ △PNR by SAS. Part (ii) extracts CM/RN = CA/RP from the Part (i) similarity and chains it with CA/RP = AB/PQ to conclude CM/RN = AB/PQ. Part (iii) gathers three equal ratio pairs CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN and concludes △CMB ∼ △RNQ by SSS similarity, completing the chain.
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: SAS and SSS similarity criteria are chained across three linked parts of Example 8 to prove that medians of similar triangles are in the same ratio as the corresponding sides.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: Throughout this chapter you have applied the AAA, SSS, and SAS similarity criteria in single-step proofs. Example 8 chains multiple similarity arguments: the result of one part becomes the input for the next. Read each part carefully and track the numbering of equations - equation labels carry forward across parts.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Complete (Part (i)):
Given: △ABC ∼ △PQR. CM is the median from C to midpoint M of AB (so AB = 2AM). RN is the median from R to midpoint N of PQ (so PQ = 2PN). Prove △AMC ∼ △PNR (see Fig. 6.33).

Solution:
Since △ABC ∼ △PQR:
AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP ... (1)
∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R ... (2)

Since AB = 2AM and PQ = 2PN (medians bisect their respective sides):
From (1): 2AM/2PN = CA/RP, so AM/PN = CA/RP ... (3)
From (2): ∠MAC = ∠NPR (both are the angle at A and P, between the respective median sides and side CA/RP) ... (4)

From (3) and (4): △AMC ∼ △PNR [SAS similarity, Theorem 6.5]. ☐

WHY SAS? The angle ∠MAC is the included angle at vertex A between sides AM (part of AB) and AC. The angle ∠NPR is the included angle at vertex P between sides PN (part of PQ) and PR. Both are included angles between the two proportional side pairs AM/PN and CA/RP.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Partially Faded (Part (ii)):
Prove that CM/RN = AB/PQ.

From part (i), △AMC ∼ △PNR, so corresponding sides give:
CM/RN = CA/RP ... (6)
But from (1): CA/RP = AB/PQ ... (7)

Your step: Combine equations (6) and (7) to write the conclusion CM/RN = AB/PQ. Label your equation (8).

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 - Further Faded (Part (iii)):
Prove that △CMB ∼ △RNQ.

From the given similarity △ABC ∼ △PQR and from part (ii):
AB/PQ = BC/QR [from (1)] and CM/RN = AB/PQ [from (8)].
Also, M is the midpoint of AB (so AB = 2BM) and N is the midpoint of PQ (so PQ = 2QN), giving CM/RN = BM/QN.

Your steps: Write the three equal ratios CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN. State which similarity criterion this satisfies. Write the formal proof that △CMB ∼ △RNQ with all steps.

CHECK: In part (i), the vertex correspondence is A↔P, M↔N, C↔R. Verify that the included angle in △AMC at vertex A is between sides AM and AC, and that the included angle in △PNR at vertex P is between sides PN and PR. Confirm the ratio equations (3) match this correspondence before applying SAS.
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Example 8 : In Fig. 6.33, CM and RN are respectively the medians of △ABC and △PQR. If △ABC ~ △PQR, prove that :
(i) △AMC ~ △PNR
(ii) CM/RN = AB/PQ
(iii) △CMB ~ △RNQ
Solution : (i) △ABC ~ △PQR (Given)
So, AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP ... (1)
and ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q and ∠C = ∠R ... (2)
But AB = 2 AM and PQ = 2 PN
(As CM and RN are medians)
So, from (1), 2AM/CA = 2PN/RP
i.e., AM/PN = CA/RP ... (3)
Also, ∠MAC = ∠NPR [From (2)] ... (4)
So, from (3) and (4),
△AMC ~ △PNR (SAS similarity) ... (5)
(ii) From (5), CM/RN = CA/RP ... (6)
But CA/RP = AB/PQ [From (1)] ... (7)
Therefore, CM/RN = AB/PQ [From (6) and (7)] ... (8)
(iii) Again, AB/PQ = BC/QR [From (1)]
Therefore, CM/RN = BC/QR [From (8)] ... (9)
Also, CM/RN = AB/PQ = 2BM/2QN
i.e., CM/RN = BM/QN ... (10)
Therefore, CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN [From (9) and (10)]
Therefore, △CMB ~ △RNQ (SSS similarity)
[Note : You can also prove part (iii) by following the same method as used for proving part (i).]
concept_bullets: The median condition AB = 2AM and PQ = 2PN allows division of the parent ratio AB/PQ = CA/RP by 2 on both numerator and denominator of the left side to obtain AM/PN = CA/RP - the key algebraic step that unlocks SAS similarity for △AMC and △PNR.

Part (ii) chains two ratio equations: CM/RN = CA/RP from the Part (i) similarity, and CA/RP = AB/PQ from the original parent similarity, giving CM/RN = AB/PQ - median ratios equal corresponding side ratios.
Part (iii) applies SSS similarity by assembling three equal ratio pairs: CM/RN = BC/QR (from Part ii and the parent similarity) and BM/QN = (AB/2)/(PQ/2) = AB/PQ = CM/RN.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: Example 8 demonstrates multi-step similarity reasoning using medians. Given △ABC ∼ △PQR with medians CM and RN, the proof of Part (i) derives AM/PN = CA/RP from the parent similarity ratio AB/PQ = CA/RP and the median condition AB = 2AM, PQ = 2PN, then combines it with ∠MAC = ∠NPR (given by the parent similarity) to conclude △AMC ∼ △PNR by SAS. Part (ii) extracts CM/RN = CA/RP from the Part (i) similarity and chains it with CA/RP = AB/PQ to conclude CM/RN = AB/PQ. Part (iii) gathers three equal ratio pairs CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN and concludes △CMB ∼ △RNQ by SSS similarity, completing the chain.
important_points: AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP
AM/PN = CA/RP
△AMC ~ △PNR (SAS similarity)
CM/RN = AB/PQ
△CMB ~ △RNQ (SSS similarity)

recall_questions.answer:
Given: △ABC ∼ △PQR, so AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP ... (1).
CM is the median from C to midpoint M of AB, so AB = 2 AM.
RN is the median from R to midpoint N of PQ, so PQ = 2 PN.

Step 1: From equation (1): AB/PQ = CA/RP.
Substitute AB = 2AM and PQ = 2PN:
2AM/2PN = CA/RP.

Step 2: Cancel the factor of 2:
AM/PN = CA/RP ... (3).

This is the required ratio equation relating the half-sides (from the medians) to the corresponding full sides.
recall_questions.prompt: In Example 8, △ABC ∼ △PQR with CM and RN as medians. Starting from the given similarity ratios, derive AM/PN = CA/RP, showing each algebraic step.

recall_questions.answer:
From Part (i): △AMC ∼ △PNR.
Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional, so:
CM/RN = CA/RP ... (6).

From the original given similarity △ABC ∼ △PQR:
CA/RP = AB/PQ ... (7) [from the common ratio in equation (1)].

Combining (6) and (7) by transitivity of equality:
CM/RN = AB/PQ. □

This is a two-step ratio chain: median CM/RN equals CA/RP from the sub-similarity, which equals AB/PQ from the original given similarity.
recall_questions.prompt: After proving △AMC ∼ △PNR (Part i of Example 8), explain how CM/RN = AB/PQ is deduced in two short steps (Part ii).

recall_questions.answer:
From the results in Parts (i) and (ii):

Step 1: CM/RN = AB/PQ [proved in Part (ii)].

Step 2: BC/QR = AB/PQ [from the original similarity △ABC ∼ △PQR].

Step 3: BM/QN = AB/PQ. Since M is the midpoint of AB: AB = 2BM. Since N is the midpoint of PQ: PQ = 2QN.
So AB/PQ = 2BM/2QN = BM/QN.

Step 4: Combine Steps 1, 2, 3:
CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN.

All three pairs of sides of △CMB and △RNQ are in the same ratio. By Theorem 6.4 (SSS Similarity Criterion), △CMB ∼ △RNQ. □

Vertex correspondence: C↔R, M↔N, B↔Q.
recall_questions.prompt: For Part (iii) of Example 8, show that CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN, and then write the similarity statement for △CMB and △RNQ with the criterion used.

STRATEGY OVERVIEW: Exercise 6.3 is the comprehensive assessment for Chapter 6, covering all five similarity criteria - AA, AAA, SSS, SAS, and the RHS criterion introduced in the Note to the Reader - across sixteen questions in varied geometric configurations. Work through questions in thematic groups; do not attempt them in isolation.

Group 1 - Identify and State (Q1, Fig. 6.34):
For each pair of triangles: inspect the given information for angle equalities or side-ratio equalities. State the criterion (AA, SSS, or SAS) and write the symbolic similarity statement with correct vertex correspondence. Incorrect vertex order is a common error - verify each correspondence before writing.

Group 2 - Angle Computation from Given Similarity (Q2, Fig. 6.35):
Given △ODC ∼ △OBA, ∠BOC = 125°, and ∠CDO = 70°. Note that ∠DOC + ∠BOC = 180° (supplementary angles on a straight line). Use angle sum of △ODC to find ∠DCO. Then use the correspondence △ODC ∼ △OBA to find ∠OAB.

WORKED EXAMPLE MODEL (Q2):
∠DOC = 180° − 125° = 55°.
In △ODC: ∠DCO = 180° − 70° − 55° = 55°.
Correspondence O↔O, D↔B, C↔A: so ∠OAB = ∠OCD = 55°? Let me restate: △ODC ∼ △OBA means ∠D = ∠B = 70° and ∠C = ∠A, so ∠OAB = ∠DCO = 55°.

Group 3 - Trapezium Diagonals (Q3):
This problem uses the same auxiliary-diagonal technique as Exercise 6.2 Q9. Draw diagonal AC of trapezium ABCD (AB ∥ DC) to create two triangles. Use AA similarity (alternate angles from AB ∥ DC) to show △OAB ∼ △OCD, then derive OA/OC = OB/OD from the corresponding-sides ratio.

Group 4 - Angle and Ratio Combinations (Q4-6):
In Q4, the condition QR/QS = QT/PR combined with ∠1 = ∠2 (∠PQS = ∠TQR) triggers SAS similarity: the equal angle ∠1 = ∠2 is the included angle between the proportional sides. Establish △PQS ∼ △TQR with careful attention to the vertex correspondence.
In Q5-6, identify two angle equalities from the stated angle conditions and apply AA.

Group 5 - Altitude Intersections (Q7, Figs. 6.37-6.38):
Altitudes AD and CE of △ABC meet at P. For each sub-part of Q7, identify two angle equalities (right angles at altitude feet, or common angles at P) and apply AA. Each sub-part uses a different triangle pair - work through each independently.

Group 6 - Parallelogram and Right-Triangle Configurations (Q8-10):
For Q8, the given congruency △ABE ≅ △ACD implies angle equalities that feed directly into AA similarity for △ADE ∼ △ABC.
For Q9, both triangles are right-angled and share a common angle - AA applies immediately. For Q10, identify the angle bisector condition and use it to set up proportional sides.

Group 7 - Synthesis and Word Problems (Q11-16):
Q11: Isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC and altitude AD ⊥ BC. Use the right angles and shared angle at A to apply AA similarity.
Q12 and Q14: These involve sides and medians of similar triangles - the same reasoning as Example 8 (Topic 14 of this chapter). Review that approach before attempting.
Q13: The condition ∠ADC = ∠BAC sets up SAS similarity between △CAD and △CBA (or equivalent pairing). From the similarity, derive CA² = CB·CD.
Q15: Indirect measurement using a pole and its shadow. This is the same technique as Example 7 (Segment 3). Draw the two triangles, identify the two right angles (vertical objects) and the common sun-angle, and apply AA.
Q16: Use the proved result that corresponding medians of similar triangles are in the same ratio as corresponding sides (Example 8, Part (ii)) to prove AB/PQ = AD/PM.

ERROR ALERT: In Q4, the vertex correspondence in △PQS ∼ △TQR requires careful attention. The angle ∠1 = ∠2 means ∠PQS = ∠TQR, so Q is the shared vertex in both triangles. The sides from Q that are proportional are QS/QR and QP/QT (note: QR/QS = QT/PR rearranges to QS/QR = QP/QT if PR = QP). Read the given ratios carefully before writing the similarity.

CHECK (Q15): A vertical pole of 6 m casts a shadow of 4 m on level ground. At the same time, a tower casts a shadow of 28 m. Draw the two similar triangles, set up the proportion, and find the height of the tower.

EXERCISE 6.3

(ii) △DCB ~ △HGE
(iii) △DCA ~ △HGF

Given: two triangles with sides in ratio 2/3 = 4/6 and an equal included angle of 50°.

The two sides are proportional (ratio 2/3) and the angle between them is equal (50° = 50°). This is exactly the SAS similarity condition.

By Theorem 6.5 (SAS Similarity Criterion), the two triangles are similar.

Let △ABC have sides AB = 2, AC = 4, ∠A = 50°, and △DEF have DE = 3, DF = 6, ∠D = 50°.
Similarity statement: △ABC ∼ △DEF.
recall_questions.prompt: In Q1 of Exercise 6.3, for a pair of triangles with sides 2 cm, 4 cm, and another pair with 3 cm, 6 cm and a common included angle of 50°, state which similarity criterion applies and write the symbolic similarity statement.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Pole height = 6 m, pole shadow = 4 m. Tower shadow = 28 m. Find tower height h.

Step 1: Both the pole and the tower are vertical (right angles with ground). Both shadows are cast by the sun simultaneously (same angle of elevation). By AA similarity, the pole-shadow triangle is similar to the tower-shadow triangle.

Step 2: Set up the proportion.
Pole height / Pole shadow = Tower height / Tower shadow
6/4 = h/28.

Step 3: Solve.
h = 6 × 28/4 = 168/4 = 42 m.

Therefore, the height of the tower is 42 m.
recall_questions.prompt: In Q15 of Exercise 6.3, a vertical pole of 6 m casts a shadow of 4 m. A tower casts a shadow of 28 m at the same time. Set up the proportion using similar triangles and find the height of the tower. Show all steps.

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1: Identify the similar triangles.
In △CAD and △CBA:
∠C = ∠C (common angle).
∠ADC = ∠BAC (given).
By AA similarity, △CAD ∼ △CBA.

Step 2: Write the corresponding-sides proportion.
From the similarity, corresponding sides are proportional:
CA/CB = CD/CA.

Step 3: Cross-multiply.
CA × CA = CB × CD
CA² = CB · CD. □

The key was recognising that ∠ADC = ∠BAC creates the second angle equality needed for AA, with ∠C being the shared angle.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
REVIEW - Chapter 6 Summary:

This chapter developed five interconnected ideas in sequence. The following nine points recap every key result.

From Segment 1 (Similar Figures and Polygon Similarity):
1. Two figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size are called similar figures.
2. All congruent figures are similar, but the converse is not true.
3. Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

From Segment 2 (Basic Proportionality Theorem):
4. Theorem 6.1 (BPT): If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
5. Theorem 6.2 (Converse BPT): If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.

From Segment 3 (Similarity Criteria for Triangles):
6. Theorem 6.3 (AAA criterion): If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are proportional and the triangles are similar.
7. AA corollary: If two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, the two triangles are similar.
8. Theorem 6.4 (SSS criterion): If in two triangles, sides of one are proportional to the sides of the other, the triangles are similar.
9. Theorem 6.5 (SAS criterion): If one angle of a triangle equals one angle of another and the sides including these angles are proportional, the triangles are similar.

NOTE TO THE READER: If in two right triangles, the hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are proportional to the hypotenuse and one side of the other triangle, then the two triangles are similar. This is the RHS Similarity Criterion.

Similarity versus congruency: Each similarity criterion has a counterpart among the congruency criteria from Class IX. The essential difference is that congruency requires equal parts (scale factor = 1) whereas similarity requires proportional parts (any scale factor). When the scale factor is exactly 1, a similarity becomes a congruency. For triangles, angle conditions alone (AAA) guarantee similarity - a property that does not extend to general polygons, as the square-and-rectangle counter-example from Segment 1 demonstrated.

CHECK: Without referring to the text, write the theorem numbers and criterion names for (a) BPT, (b) Converse BPT, (c) AAA similarity, (d) SSS similarity, and (e) SAS similarity. Then verify against the summary above.

6.5 Summary
In this chapter you have studied the following points :
1. Two figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size are called similar figures.
2. All the congruent figures are similar but the converse is not true.
3. Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (i.e., proportion).
4. If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, then the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
5. If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
6. If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio and hence the two triangles are similar (AAA similarity criterion).
7. If in two triangles, two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to the two angles of the other triangle, then the two triangles are similar (AA similarity criterion).
8. If in two triangles, corresponding sides are in the same ratio, then their corresponding angles are equal and hence the triangles are similar (SSS similarity criterion).
9. If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and the sides including these angles are in the same ratio (proportional), then the triangles are similar (SAS similarity criterion).
NOTE TO THE READER
If in two right triangles, hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are proportional to the hypotenuse and one side of the other triangle, then the two triangles are similar. This may be referred to as the RHS Similarity Criterion.
If you use this criterion in Example 2, Chapter 8, the proof will become simpler.
concept_bullets: All nine results of Chapter 6 form a logical chain: the definition of similarity underpins the polygon conditions, the polygon conditions specialise to triangles, BPT enables the proofs of the similarity criteria, and the criteria are used in all application problems.

The SAS similarity criterion (Theorem 6.5) differs from SAS congruency only in the side requirement - proportional sides (ratio k) versus equal sides (ratio 1) - while both require the equal angle to be the included angle between those sides.

The RHS similarity criterion applies exclusively to right triangles: if the hypotenuse and one leg of one right triangle are proportional to the hypotenuse and corresponding leg of another, the triangles are similar - for example, right triangles with hypotenuse 5 cm and leg 3 cm, and hypotenuse 10 cm and leg 6 cm, are similar by RHS.

A Note to the Reader adds the RHS Similarity Criterion for right triangles. The review compares each similarity criterion with its congruency counterpart from Class IX, establishing that the essential difference is proportional sides in similarity versus equal sides in congruency, with the angle conditions preserved in both. When the scale factor equals 1, similarity becomes congruency.

Theorem 6.3 (AAA Similarity Criterion): If in two triangles, all three pairs of corresponding angles are equal, then the triangles are similar.

Theorem 6.4 (SSS Similarity Criterion): If in two triangles, all three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional (in the same ratio), then the triangles are similar.

Theorem 6.5 (SAS Similarity Criterion): If one pair of corresponding angles are equal and the sides including those angles are proportional, then the triangles are similar.
recall_questions.prompt: Without referring to your notes, state the three similarity criteria for triangles (Theorems 6.3, 6.4, and 6.5) in one sentence each, including their theorem numbers and commonly used names.

recall_questions.answer:
Essential difference: In SAS congruency (Class IX), the two sides must be EQUAL in length (scale factor = 1). In SAS similarity (Theorem 6.5), the two sides must be PROPORTIONAL (any scale factor k), not necessarily equal.

Condition that remains the same: In both cases, the angle condition is identical - the equal angle must be the INCLUDED angle, lying between the two sides being compared.

Summary: SAS congruency checks AB = DE and AC = DF with ∠A = ∠D (included). SAS similarity checks AB/DE = AC/DF (same ratio, not necessarily 1) with ∠A = ∠D (included). Congruency is the special case of similarity when the scale factor is exactly 1.
